amr-kernel.summary: Wavelet-error-driven octree adaptive-mesh-refinement (AMR) time-evolution of the BSSN formulation of the Einstein field equations (binary-black-hole merger, gravitational-wave generation), benchmarked with the paper's own regrid-cost-vs-solve-cost profiling decomposition (remsh_igt vs. rhs/evolve) rather than a synthetic uniform-grid correctness reference, since this track's sole paper's own repo has no such bundled reference script (survey.md Divergences #3).
amr-kernel.operation: for each of NT RK4 sub-timesteps: (1) Regrid -- re-evaluate the wavelet refinement criterion on the current solution and refine/coarsen octants where the estimated wavelet coefficient crosses BSSN_WAVELET_TOL (with BSSN_DENDRO_AMR_FAC coarsening hysteresis), performed every BSSN_REMESH_TEST_FREQ steps, not every step; (2) Unzip -- convert the distributed octree (compressed-graph) representation to zero-padded ghosted patches ("octant-to-patch"), optionally overlapped with the corresponding MPI ghost-exchange; (3) RHS -- evaluate the 6th-order finite-difference BSSN right-hand side on every patch; (4) Zip -- convert patches back to the octree representation ("patch-to-octant"); repeat (2)-(4) 4x per RK4 sub-step. Periodically (BSSN_GW_EXTRACT_FREQ), extract psi4 gravitational-wave modes at 6 fixed observer radii.

variants.claim: steady-state per-timestep cost broken into regrid vs. solve vs. data- layout-conversion phases, matching the paper's own profiling-field decomposition exactly (survey.md: remsh_igt / unzip+comm / rhs / zip), at a fixed, reduced problem size runnable on a single GPU or CPU node -- NOT the full production q=1 config (which targets a full supercomputer allocation), since a single-node kernel-level variant needs a problem size within reach of one node

strong- and weak-scaling behavior with the regrid-cost fraction (remsh_igt / evolve) reported explicitly as a function of scale, since this track's paper's central claim is GPU acceleration AT SCALE (up to 8 A100s strong scaling, up to 229,376 x86 cores weak scaling per the abstract), not single-node throughput alone -- included as a second variant specifically so the scaling claim is independently checkable, matching this project's pattern of a kernel-only + a scaling/e2e variant per track

ann-search.summary: Nearest-neighbor search over a fixed vector/point database, split into two variants that the 7 surveyed papers treat as genuinely different claims: high-dimensional APPROXIMATE search over the standard SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV billion-scale suite (recall@k vs QPS Pareto curve as THE metric, never QPS alone), and low-dimensional (2D/3D) EXACT (or tightly error-bounded) spatial k-NN over real point-cloud/geometric data where recall@k is meaningless (search is exact by construction) and correctness is instead a measured exact-match rate or bounded error rate. Index-build time/memory and batch-vs-single-query latency are always reported separately from steady-state search throughput in both variants.
ann-search.operation: high-dim variant: for each query q in Q[Nq,D], return the (approximate) top-k indices of X[N,D] minimizing dist(q, x_i) under a fixed distance metric (L2 by default), N up to 10^9, D in [96,128]; low-dim/exact variant: for each query q in Q[Nq,D], return the EXACT top-k (or all points within a fixed radius r) of X[N,D], D in {2,3}, N up to 10^7

variants.claim: steady-state approximate nearest-neighbor search throughput (QPS) at FIXED recall@k targets, reported as a recall-vs-QPS curve (never QPS alone), with index-build time and peak memory reported as separate, one-shot numbers (not amortized into per-query time). This is the common denominator PathWeaver, DRIM-ANN, UpANNS, and FANNS all actually target (all 4 evaluate on the SIFT/DEEP/SPACEV billion-scale family and an IVF-PQ-or-graph-based index), and is the standard ann-benchmarks.com-style framing this track's papers only partially realize on their own (see Divergences: only FANNS sweeps multiple recall targets by construction; the other 3 report at most one fixed recall floor or none at all in their released scripts).

steady-state EXACT (or, if the candidate is RTNN-style radius-relaxation approximate, tightly error-bounded with the error rate measured and reported as a first-class number, not assumed) k-nearest-neighbor or fixed-radius search over low-dimensional (2D/3D) point data, preprocessing (spatial index/BVH/grid construction) excluded and reported separately. This is CLOVER's and RTNN's own claim, and what X-HD's internal RT-accelerated k-NN routine (not its end-to-end Hausdorff-distance computation, which is a different operation) is a valid candidate submission for. Recall@k does not apply here — accuracy is binary exact-match (or a measured approximation-error rate for RTNN-style candidates), not a ratio against an approximate baseline.

astar-search.summary: Single-pair shortest-path search (start -> goal) on an 8-connected 2D occupancy grid via GPU-parallel (bidirectional or unidirectional) bucketed A*, measured as search-phase wall time and nodes expanded, with path optimality (not approximation) as the correctness gate.
astar-search.operation: path = A*(grid[H,W] occupancy (0=passable,1=obstacle), start, goal, heuristic=octile/Chebyshev-consistent); 8-connected movement, integer- scaled edge costs (straight vs. diagonal); output is the minimum-cost path (or "unreachable") plus the parent chain from start to goal.

variants.claim: steady-state search-phase throughput on the standard MovingAI pathfinding benchmark corpus; grid/scenario loading excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

steady-state search-phase throughput on the repo's own parameterized procedural-grid generator, sweeping obstacle family and grid size — the axis the paper itself uses to show the bucketed-bidirectional design scaling with grid complexity

attention-kernel.summary: Fused scaled-dot-product attention (the softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V core of transformer models), measured as steady-state kernel throughput with preprocessing (QKV projection, RoPE, KV-cache paging/block-table setup) reported separately, split into prefill/full-sequence, decode/KV-cache, and CPU-multicore variants that the surveyed literature treats as genuinely different claims — plus a causal-vs-bidirectional mask axis and an fp16/bf16 precision axis within each GPU variant.
attention-kernel.operation: O[B,H,Sq,d] = softmax( (Q[B,H,Sq,d] @ K[B,Hkv,Sk,d]^T) / sqrt(d) + mask ) @ V[B,Hkv,Sk,d]   (GQA when Hkv < H; MHA when Hkv == H; Sq == Sk for prefill, Sq == 1 for decode)

variants.claim: steady-state fused forward-pass attention kernel throughput for prefill/training-style workloads (all of Q attends over all of K,V in one call; no incremental KV cache), preprocessing (QKV projection, RoPE application, mask/bias construction) excluded and reported separately. This is the common denominator ByteTransformer, E.T., Hexcute's `benchmark_attention.py`, and FlashAttention-T's Figure-8 comparison all actually measure, and what RedFuser's MHA/MLA cascaded- reduction fusion and MetaAttention's generated softmax-attention kernel are drop-in candidates for.

steady-state single-query decode attention kernel throughput against a KV cache — memory-bandwidth-bound, always causal, GQA-heavy. This is PAT's primary claim and one of Hexcute's two attention benchmarks (`benchmark_flash_decoding.py`); FlashAttention/FlashInfer/vLLM-FA and the other prefix-aware baselines (FastTree, RelayAttention, DeFT, Cascade Inference) that PAT compares against all target exactly this operation.

steady-state CPU-multicore fused attention kernel throughput, fp32, full physical core count, full-sequence self-attention (no KV-cache decode). The CPU analogue of attn-prefill-kernel — MEATTEN's ARM target is the only CPU paper in this track, so this variant also defines the fairness fixes needed on top of MEATTEN's own (loose) released protocol.

autotuner-multi-kernel.summary: Unlike the other tracks in this project, the "kernel" under test here is a compiler/autotuner SYSTEM, not a single fixed operation: the system is given a fixed, named multi-kernel suite (dense DL/HPC linear algebra, sparse linear algebra, and PolyBench affine loops) plus a search budget, and is scored on BOTH the wall-clock cost to reach a schedule/kernel AND the steady-state performance of the kernel that schedule produces — since the surveyed literature reports these two axes with wildly inconsistent rigor (see survey.md "Divergences"), and this track's own name ("multi-kernel") signals that suite breadth, not single-kernel depth, is the point.
autotuner-multi-kernel.operation: system-under-test S (a compiler, autotuner, or scheduling-language instance) is given each kernel k in the fixed suite K below, as source/IR, plus a wall-clock search budget; S produces optimized executable code for k; both the search trajectory (time -> best-found performance) and the final produced code's steady-state performance are measured. K spans three disjoint kernel families (dense/sparse tensor ops, PolyBench affine loops) because the surveyed papers target genuinely different substrates and optimizing across them is not a single comparable operation.

variants.claim: post-tuning steady-state kernel throughput of the dense+sparse tensor kernel suite, fp32, using whichever schedule the system under test found within the tensor-kernel-tuning-cost variant's 3600s checkpoint (search time is EXCLUDED from this number but its cap is enforced — unlike GMC/PrecTuner/WACO/FlexTensor, which report post-tuning numbers with no reported/bounded search budget at all).

the search/tuning cost required to reach the steady-state variant's result, reported as a Pareto curve (time -> best-found performance) at fixed checkpoints — mandatory and primary as WALL-CLOCK time, because the track's own papers use incommensurable units (Pruner: trial count; TPP-mlir: wall time; CuAsmRL: "one-time training cost"; WACO/GMC: unreported despite search/model-solve being their core contribution).

steady-state execution time of the PolyBench/C 4.2.1 suite (fixed 30-kernel list, LARGE_DATASET), the one input family this track's literature is directly and confirmably anchored to (PrecTuner/LnLAMP) — kept as its own variant rather than folded into the tensor-kernel variants because PolyBench's kernels (stencils, DP recurrences like nussinov/floyd-warshall, solvers) are not FLOP-throughput-comparable to GEMM/conv, and PolyBench papers customarily report raw time + speedup, not GFLOP/s.

precision-vs-speed Pareto frontier for the subset of PolyBench kernels amenable to mixed/reduced precision (PrecTuner's own target: nussinov, fdtd-2d, heat-3d, seidel-2d, plus any kernel the system under test chooses to lower) — reported as a FRONTIER, not gated by a single fixed tolerance, because PrecTuner's own design explicitly trades accuracy for speed under a tunable error budget, unlike the fixed-dtype half-precision variants used elsewhere in this track (Pruner/CuAsmRL/ TPP-mlir simply run a kernel in fp16; PrecTuner tunes A CONTINUOUS precision-selection parameter).

batched-gemm.summary: Batched GEMM: many independent small-to-medium matrix multiplications launched as a single batched/grouped operation, covering both the uniform-shape case (every batch element is the same [M,K]x[K,N]) and the variable-shape/segmented ("grouped GEMM") case that this track's one surveyed paper (FASTEN) targets, where each of T segments has its own row-count M_i sharing a common K and per-segment weight [K,N].
batched-gemm.operation: uniform: C_b[M,N] = A_b[M,K] * B_b[K,N] for b in 0..batch-1 (independent, no cross-batch reuse). variable/segmented: given data[sum(M_i), K] and T per-type weights W_t[K,N], C[sum(M_i), N] where rows belonging to segment i are multiplied by W_{type(i)}; forward and backward (dC/dA, dC/dW) are both in scope, since FASTEN benchmarks both.

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput of uniform-shape batched GEMM (same M,N,K across the whole batch), preprocessing excluded. Not directly evidenced by FASTEN's own artifact (which targets the variable-shape case) but included as the natural counterpart the track's axis list requires ("uniform vs variable batch"); shapes and K values below are taken from FASTEN's own benchmarked feature widths so the two variants stay comparable on K.

steady-state kernel throughput of variable-shape/segmented ("grouped") GEMM on real per-type segment-size distributions, forward and backward, preprocessing (engine/format dispatch) excluded but reported. This is FASTEN's own actual benchmark shape and is kept as its own variant rather than folded into batched-gemm-uniform-kernel because the per-segment row count M_i varies (irregular workload distribution across the batch), which materially changes load-balancing behavior relative to the uniform case.

betweenness.summary: Single-source dependency-accumulation betweenness centrality on hypergraphs (Brandes-style forward BFS + backward dependency phases, generalized from vertices/edges to vertices/hyperedges), measured as wall-clock running time and parallel self-speedup on a shared-memory multicore machine; hypergraph load time excluded from per-round timing.
betweenness.operation: dep[V] = HyperBC(H=(V,E) hypergraph, source in V); H is unweighted, undirected (symmetric) incidence structure between vertices and hyperedges; output is a per-vertex dependency/centrality score (double) accumulated via one forward traversal (shortest-hyperpath counting) and one backward traversal (dependency propagation) from a single source vertex — same scope as classical single-source Brandes BC, not an all-pairs/exact aggregate BC.

variants.claim: steady-state single-source HyperBC running time and multicore speedup on named real-world hypergraphs; hypergraph load/parse excluded from per-round timing but reported separately, once

cost of hypergraph construction (format conversion from raw SNAP/KONECT source) reported standalone, plus the thread-count scaling curve from 1 to 144 threads on a single fixed hypergraph — operationalizes the paper's own Figure 2 (varying threads) as a first-class variant rather than folding it into the single-source kernel-only number

bfs.summary: Breadth-first search from a set of source vertices over a directed or undirected graph in CSR/CSC form, measured as traversed-edges-per-second with preprocessing (format conversion, reordering, bitmap construction) strictly separated from per-search kernel time.
bfs.operation: parent[V] = BFS(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR), source in V); A is unweighted (or weight-agnostic — only connectivity matters); output is a parent/predecessor array (or level array) over all V vertices, undefined (INT64_MAX-sentinel) for unreached vertices.

variants.claim: steady-state search-phase throughput on synthetic Graph500 R-MAT graphs; graph generation and CSR construction excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

steady-state search-phase throughput on named real-world graphs, union of the graph families actually used across the track's papers; same protocol as bfs-kernel-rmat-graph500 but on fixed, disambiguated real instances instead of a parameterized generator

end-to-end throughput including one-shot preprocessing (CSR conversion, any graph reordering, and any specialized layout/bitmap construction), amortized over k=64 searches — the same k as the kernel-only variants' repetition count, so the amortization argument is apples-to-apples with the kernel-only numbers rather than an arbitrarily chosen k

cost/benefit of a graph-reordering preprocessing step on its own terms: reordering wall time, resulting kernel speedup on a downstream BFS, and the break-even repetition count — operationalizes Corder's own amortization discipline as a first-class, reportable variant instead of an implicit footnote, and gives reordering-focused papers (Corder, RCM) a variant that measures what they actually contribute

bipartite-matching.summary: Exact maximum-cardinality matching in bipartite graphs on GPU via a deterministic initial-matching phase followed by parallel bidirectional augmenting-path search, measured as steady-state edges/s throughput with the two algorithmic phases (initial matching, augmenting-path search) timed and reported separately since the code itself already separates them rather than blending into one number.
bipartite-matching.operation: match[V] = MaxBipartiteMatching(A[L,R] biadjacency (sparse, CSR, unweighted), L,R the two vertex partitions); output is a partial bijection between L and R such that every matched pair is an edge in A and no vertex is matched more than once; the algorithm returns a MAXIMUM-cardinality such matching (exact, not approximate).

variants.claim: steady-state augmenting-path-search-phase throughput on the paper's own 21-graph SuiteSparse suite, treated as bipartite (rows vs. columns, or the graph's natural bipartite structure where applicable); Matrix-Market-to-CSR conversion excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

head-to-head comparison against the fastest prior CPU and fastest prior GPU maximum-bipartite-matching codes on the SAME 21-instance suite, elevated to its own variant since it requires matched baseline builds rather than being a standalone ECL-MM number, and is the paper's own headline claim (4.5x vs. fastest prior CPU code, speedup factor vs. fastest prior GPU code — exact GPU factor not confirmed from available sources, see open_questions)

blas-level1-2.summary: Vector-vector (level-1: dot, axpy, nrm2, scal) and matrix-vector (level-2: gemv, symmetric symv, triangular trsv) BLAS operations, as produced by the compiler/DSL/generator systems this track's 4 papers actually are (only 1 of 4, fBLAS, benchmarks named BLAS routines directly against a reference library the other way this spec's other tracks do; the other 3 evaluate a generator whose output includes BLAS-L1/L2-shaped kernels among a broader kernel set — see survey.md Divergences). Overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth-bound at every vector/matrix length large enough to exceed L1 cache, so GB/s is this track's primary metric, same as the gemv track.
blas-level1-2.operation: level-1: r = sum_i(x_i*y_i) [dot], y = a*x+y [axpy], r = ||x||_2 [nrm2], x = a*x [scal]. level-2: y = alpha*A*x + beta*y [gemv, A general MxK]; y = alpha*A*x + beta*y [symv, A symmetric MxM, only the canonical upper- or lower-triangle stored/read — half the memory traffic of a general gemv at the same M, a genuine byte-accounting difference this spec's metric formulas must reflect, not just a different access pattern]; x = A^-1*x [trsv, A triangular — NOT evidenced in any of this track's 4 surveyed papers, kept as an explicitly out-of-evidence optional op, see open_questions].

variants.claim: steady-state bandwidth for level-1 vector ops (dot, axpy, nrm2, scal) across a vector-length sweep spanning L1 through DRAM- resident working sets, with an explicit reduction-accuracy axis for the two reduction ops (dot, nrm2) — the common-denominator variant, grounded directly in fBLAS's own `sdot`/`ddot` evaluation harness (`evaluation/individual_modules/`, `evaluation/cpu_comparison/host_dot.cpp`), the only paper in this track whose level-1 benchmark code was read in full.

steady-state bandwidth for level-2 matrix-vector ops, covering both general GEMV (fBLAS's `sgemv`/`dgemv`) and symmetry-exploiting SYMV (SySTeC's `ssymv`, which reads only the canonical triangle) at matched M — the pairing exists specifically to make the symmetric-storage bandwidth *reduction* (not just a different access pattern) a first-class, measured comparison rather than two unrelated numbers, since that reduction is exactly what SySTeC's own compiler is built to automatically exploit.

measured (not merely instruction-count-estimated) runtime throughput of a mixed-precision, integer-accumulated dot-product reduction targeting fused dot-product ISA extensions (AVX512-VNNI and equivalents) — grounded in VeGen's own `dot_16x1x16_uint8_int8_int32` benchmark kernel, but this spec REQUIRES an actual wall-clock/cycle-accurate measurement rather than the static instruction-count comparison VeGen's own recovered evaluation figure appears to use (see survey.md, "Timing protocol... not recoverable" and the inference that VeGen's evaluation may be closer to a static-cost-model comparison for at least some reported numbers) — a fairness fix this spec makes explicitly, not a reproduction of an unconfirmed practice, since instruction count does not account for issue-width, port contention, or memory-system effects that a real dot-product kernel's throughput depends on.

aggregate throughput and correctness across a BROAD suite of compiler/DSL-generated level-1/2 (and adjacent) kernels compared against the same vendor-BLAS reference set — the variant this track most needs given that 3 of its 4 papers (Exo 2, SySTeC, and to a lesser extent VeGen) are fundamentally "benchmark a generator across many kernels" rather than "benchmark one named routine", unlike fBLAS and unlike the gemv track's papers. Exo 2's own claim ("comparable to or better than MKL, OpenBLAS, BLIS... on AVX2, AVX512, and Gemmini") is exactly this shape of claim; this variant's protocol exists to make that claim independently checkable per-kernel rather than only as an aggregate statement, since no per-kernel breakdown for the BLAS L1/2 subset specifically was recoverable from the sources read in this pass (see survey.md open_questions).

cellular-automata.summary: GPU cellular-automaton (CA) time-stepping throughput for the Larger-Than-Life (LTL) family, where the transition function is a weighted summation over an r-cell-radius neighborhood; compares a tensor-core-mapped implementation against CUDA-core baselines (naive, coarsened, shared-memory-tiled, bit-packed) sharing one codebase, across a radius sweep since radius is the axis the paper's own contribution targets.
cellular-automata.operation: Given an N x N x Z boolean/low-integer grid (Z independent layers simulated in parallel) and radius r, each step computes for every cell a weighted sum of its (2r+1)x(2r+1) neighborhood and applies a birth/survival threshold rule (LTL: alive iff the sum falls in a configured interval, generalizing Conway's Game of Life to r>1); iterated for `steps` timesteps with periodic or fixed boundary halo handling.

variants.claim: steady-state per-step kernel throughput (cell-updates/s) as a function of neighborhood radius r, one-shot data layout preparation (uint8 -> tensor-core / bit-packed layout) excluded from per-step time and reported separately, since the artifact's own harness already performs this separation and radius is the paper's central independent variable.

effect of fusing k CA steps into one kernel launch (CATMultiStepSolver / CATMultiStepSolver2 vs single-step CATSolver) on halo-exchange amortization, isolating a second axis (fusion depth) the paper's own three tensor-core variants target independently of the radius sweep.

cg-krylov.summary: Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (and closely related nested/mixed- precision Krylov variants) for sparse symmetric positive-definite linear systems A x = b; measured as four distinct claims this track's own artifacts already draw different lines around — a fixed-iteration unpreconditioned kernel-throughput variant (PERKS's own research question), an end-to-end to-convergence ILU(0)-preconditioned variant with mandatory separate preconditioner-setup reporting (generalizing SPCG's own good practice), a synthetic HPCG-style 3D-stencil-generator + AMG-preconditioned distributed/weak-scaling variant (BootCMatchGX, Graphene, and CLAIRE all use a generator instead of a downloaded matrix), and a reduced-precision cascade variant (F3R, Mille-feuille) that requires an independent fp64-accuracy gate rather than trusting the low-precision recurrence's own residual.
cg-krylov.operation: solve A x = b (A sparse, real, symmetric positive-definite, N x N) via (preconditioned) Conjugate Gradient. One PCG iteration = 1 SpMV (q = A*p) + optional preconditioner apply (z = M^-1*r) + 2 dot-product reductions + 3 AXPY-family vector updates (p = z + beta*p; x = x + alpha*p; r = r - alpha*q).

variants.claim: steady-state per-iteration cost of the UNPRECONDITIONED CG kernel (SpMV + 2 dots + 3 axpys), fixed iteration count, preconditioner excluded entirely — isolates the CG kernel itself from any preconditioner-specific behavior, matching PERKS's explicit research question (persistent-kernel throughput for iterative memory-bound solvers). Fixes two things found in this track's own artifacts: (1) PERKS's own single CUDA-event bracket spanning ALL iterations (divided by iteration count afterward) is replaced with genuine per-iteration timestamps, and (2) the iteration count used in any derived per-iteration number must be read back from the actual loop counter, not a hardcoded literal — the exact bug found in Mille-feuille's public artifact (loop always runs a hardcoded 10000 iterations regardless of the `maxiter` argument, and the reported time is divided by a literal 100, not the true iteration count or a variable).

end-to-end time-to-solution for ILU(0)-preconditioned CG run to a relative-residual convergence gate, with preconditioner analysis+factorization ALWAYS measured and reported separately from the PCG loop — generalizes SPCG's own artifact discipline (which gets this right in the one file surveyed) into a mandatory requirement for every submission, since no other surveyed paper in this track implements this exact ILU(0)+CG configuration to compare against directly.

to-convergence throughput on synthetic HPCG-style 3D-stencil SPD systems (generated in-memory, not downloaded), AMG-preconditioned, reported as weak- and strong-scaling curves — targets the distributed/multi-node usage pattern that a fixed downloaded matrix cannot represent, and which THREE independently-surveyed papers on three different platforms actually use (BootCMatchGX's `--laplacian-3d SIZE --laplacian-3d-generator 7p|27p` on multi-GPU MPI, F3R's locally-generated `hpcg_<nx>_<ny>_<nz>.mtx`, and Graphene's `-p/--poisson nx,ny,nz` on IPU) — confirming this is a real methodological split in the track's own literature, not a spec-author invention.

to-convergence solve using a reduced-precision cascade (fp64 outer / fp32-or-fp16 inner), reporting speedup vs. a matched fp64-only baseline WITHOUT silently trading away final accuracy — targets F3R's nested FGMRES/Richardson fp16-inner design and Mille-feuille's tile-grained on-chip dynamic precision conversion, the two papers in this track that build reduced-precision Krylov solvers as their central contribution.

cholesky.summary: Dense/tile Cholesky factorization of a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix (or covariance operator), spanning four claims this track's own literature treats as genuinely different: plain dense fp64 tile Cholesky (single-node and distributed/communication-optimal), tile low-rank (TLR) Cholesky for formally-dense but data-sparse operators, and mixed/adaptive- precision (FP64/FP32/FP16/FP8, plus INT8 for a non-Cholesky sub-kernel) tile Cholesky on CPU and GPU tensor cores.
cholesky.operation: A[N,N] (SPD) = L[N,N] * L[N,N]^T, tile-blocked (block size NB, tile count N/NB per dimension); TLR variants additionally compress off-diagonal tiles to rank <= r under an accuracy threshold before/while factoring; mixed- precision variants cast individual tiles or diagonal bands to a lower precision before the same tile-blocked factorization.

variants.claim: steady-state single-node (shared-memory) dense tile Cholesky factorization time, fp64, with tile size (NB) as a required, per-run-disclosed parameter rather than a silently fixed constant — the single clearest lesson from KwasniewskiKBZS21 (paper 1 in the survey), where 3 of 4 baselines only beat COnfLUX/COnfCHOX after the paper's authors hand-tuned NB. Matrix generation is preprocessing, excluded from the timed region but reported once. This is the entry point most reproducible without a multi-node allocation; it is smaller in scope than the distributed variant below because most of this track's own papers (paper 1-paper 5, paper 8) only report distributed-scale numbers even though the underlying binaries (hicma-x's testing_potrf_tlr, exageostat's dmle drivers) run on 1 node.

distributed (multi-node) dense tile Cholesky at scale, reporting both time-to-solution and aggregate communication volume, with block size AND process grid (P x Q) as required disclosed parameters — this is the variant KwasniewskiKBZS21 (paper 1) is purpose-built for, and the one where the whole track's tile-size-tuning divergence (see notes_on_fairness) is most consequential, since 3 of 4 of paper 1's own baselines are only competitive after manual tuning.

tile low-rank (TLR) Cholesky factorization of a formally-dense, data-sparse SPD operator (covariance matrix or 3D RBF-interpolation operator), with TLR accuracy threshold AND tile size both required, swept, disclosed parameters. Compression (dense->TLR) time is measured and reported separately from factorization, following paper 2's own practice of showing compression can dominate once factorization itself is fast.

mixed/adaptive-precision tile Cholesky (FP64/FP32/FP16/FP8, CPU or GPU tensor-core), with the precision-ASSIGNMENT STRATEGY itself (not just the resulting FP64/FP32/FP16/FP8 fractions) as a required, disclosed parameter, since paper 3/paper 4's band-percentage scheme and paper 6's tile-centric adaptive-decision scheme are structurally different rules that happen to produce comparable-looking fraction numbers — reporting only the fractions without the assignment rule would make cross-paper comparison meaningless (the same lesson as paper 1's tile-size finding, generalized to precision assignment).

climate-kernel.summary: Throughput of two structurally unrelated climate-adjacent kernels this track's 2 papers actually cover: (1) a Tensor-Core-accelerated shallow-water dynamical-core stencil (pure fluid dynamics, no physics parameterization), and (2) a mixed-precision spherical-harmonic-transform + tile-low-rank Cholesky kernel underlying a statistical climate emulator (no dynamics at all — emulates ensemble statistics of prior GCM output). No shared input suite or metric is imposed across the two; each gets its own variant reflecting what its own paper actually measures. Grid-size/timing conventions for variant 1 are shared with `benchspecs/stencil/spec.yaml` (same paper, ozHOPE, cross-listed in both tracks).
climate-kernel.operation: Variant 1: U_out[p] = convolution-reformulated shallow-water stencil update at grid point p on a spherical/latitude-longitude domain, for T timesteps, computed via FP16 Tensor-Core MMA with Ozaki-scheme precision restoration. Variant 2: given N=L^2 spatio-temporal sample points (L = latitude resolution), compute forward spherical-harmonic transform -> SYRK covariance matrix C=AA^T -> mixed-precision tile-low-rank Cholesky factorization of C (repeated nruns times) -> inverse SHT -> MSE against a reference; the emulator's usable output is one statistical field realization per forward-factor-inverse pass.

variants.claim: End-to-end speedup of a Tensor-Core-accelerated shallow-water dynamical core over its FP64 (or working-precision) baseline on the Williamson standard atmospheric-dynamics test suite, with accuracy order-of-convergence preserved and reported ALONGSIDE speedup, never substituted for it. Reused from `benchspecs/stencil/spec.yaml`'s ozHOPE entry (same paper); reframed here around this track's own dynamics-only framing.

Throughput of the mixed-precision SHT + tile-low-rank Cholesky kernel underlying a statistical climate emulator, with the one-shot forward-SHT/SYRK/matrix-norm phases reported separately (never amortized into the per-run factorization time) and the factorization phase itself repeated nruns times — the harness's OWN native preprocessing/kernel split (survey.md Divergence 4), adopted verbatim rather than imposed from outside.

community-detection.summary: Discover a partition of a graph's vertices into communities that (for the Louvain-family variants) maximizes modularity, measured as wall-clock time to convergence with the resulting partition's quality reported jointly and gated — a faster run that converges to a materially worse partition does not count as an improvement. A separate variant covers the track's two non-modularity algorithm families (structural-entropy optimization, single-pass threshold clustering) so their real contributions remain benchmarkable without conflating them with modularity-comparable numbers.
community-detection.operation: C[V] = CommunityDetection(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR/edge-list), weighted or unweighted); output is a vertex-to-community-ID labeling over all V vertices; for Louvain-family variants the labeling is produced by iterating (local-move phase to a modularity-gain threshold) then (community aggregation into a coarser graph) until no further gain; number of communities is DISCOVERED, not a caller-supplied parameter (this is the key structural difference from the graph-partitioning track).

variants.claim: steady-state Louvain-family (modularity-maximizing) community detection kernel time on a fixed real-graph suite, with final modularity reported jointly and gated: a run whose modularity falls below the quality floor is disqualified from the throughput ranking regardless of how fast it completed

end-to-end throughput including one-shot graph loading and CSR/adjacency-list construction; community detection is inherently single-shot per input (no repeated-query amortization argument the way BFS or SpMV have), so this variant reports ONE full run's total time rather than an amortized-over-k number

dedicated measurement of run-to-run partition variance under a fixed thread/GPU count and fixed input — directly operationalizes NiuOSC26's own subject matter (existing parallel Louvain implementations lack a convergence guarantee and can converge to different local optima across runs due to concurrent stale-data reads) as a first-class, reportable variant instead of an implicit assumption

time, memory, and the algorithm's OWN native objective value for the track's two non-modularity algorithm families (HSSInfo's structural- entropy minimization, ProbGraph's approximate Jarvis-Patrick threshold clustering) — explicitly NOT cross-comparable in a throughput ranking against cd-kernel-modularity's modularity-gated numbers, since these algorithms are answering different questions; where feasible, ALSO compute post-hoc modularity of the resulting partition so a reader can cross-reference the two axes without the spec falsely implying the numbers are interchangeable

connected-components.summary: Connectivity-decomposition kernels on graphs (or, for one sub-problem, regular pixel/voxel grids), covering the three genuinely distinct sub-problems this track's own papers actually evaluate: biconnected components (BCC, undirected), strongly connected components (SCC, directed), and binary-image 2D/3D connected-component labeling (CCL, regular grid, not a general sparse graph). Each sub-problem gets its own variant family rather than being forced into a single shared shape, since their operations, correctness definitions, and even connectivity semantics ("8-connectivity" vs. "strongly reachable" vs. "removal of one vertex disconnects") are not interchangeable.
connected-components.operation: BCC: label[V], componentHead[label] = BCC(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, symmetric/undirected CSR)); label[v] identifies which biconnected component each non-root vertex's incident tree edge belongs to, and the set of cut vertices/cut edges is derivable from label[] and componentHead[] in O(1) per query. SCC: scc_id[V] = SCC(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, DIRECTED CSR)); scc_id[v] identifies the strongly-connected component containing v, such that contracting each scc_id-class to a single vertex yields a DAG. Image-CCL: label[H,W] (2D) or label[D,H,W] (3D) = CCL(image[H,W] or [D,H,W] (binary, foreground/background)); label assigns a unique positive integer to every maximal foreground blob under a fixed connectivity rule (8-connectivity for 2D, 26-connectivity for 3D), 0 for background.

variants.claim: steady-state biconnected-components kernel time on named undirected real-world graphs that fit in device/node memory, with the internal connected-components subroutine's algorithm family (Shiloach-Vishkin pointer-jumping vs. Afforest/k-out-sampling vs. other) mandatorily disclosed, since both surveyed BCC papers show this subroutine choice is consequential to reported performance

biconnected-components cost when the input graph exceeds accelerator memory, requiring a batched/external-memory algorithm — makes FAST-BCC-Filter/PEA-BCC's out-of-memory contribution a first-class, separately-reportable variant rather than folding it into the in-memory variant's numbers, since the two are not comparable without disclosing the memory-constraint regime each was measured under

steady-state strongly-connected-components kernel time on named DIRECTED real-world and domain-specific graphs, with the algorithm-family (max-ID-propagation vs. Forward-Backward/BFS-pivot vs. spanning-tree+relaxed-sync) mandatorily disclosed, and with graph REGIME (power-law vs. structured/mesh) treated as a first- class axis since the one surveyed paper shows speedup is strongly regime-dependent rather than a single blanket number

steady-state binary-image connected-component-labeling kernel time on named real image datasets, under a fixed connectivity rule (8-connectivity 2D / 26-connectivity 3D), with the underlying algorithm family and the specific test axis (plain average runtime vs. density/granularity/blocksize sensitivity) both disclosed — this variant is explicitly scoped to a REGULAR-GRID sub-problem, not the general sparse-graph connectivity this spec's other 3 variants cover, and inherits the surveyed paper's own richer, multi-axis test taxonomy rather than collapsing it to a single number

content-defined-chunking.summary: SIMD-vectorized content-defined chunking (CDC) for data deduplication: scan a byte stream and emit content-determined chunk boundaries (so identical content re-aligns to identical chunks regardless of insertions/deletions elsewhere in the stream), measured as throughput JOINTLY with achieved average chunk size and deduplication space savings on a real dataset -- never throughput alone, since a degenerate boundary rule (e.g. always chunk at a fixed offset) trivially maximizes throughput while destroying dedup ratio.
content-defined-chunking.operation: Given a byte stream of length N and target average chunk size C_avg (with configured min/max bounds C_min, C_max): scan the stream once, left to right, and at each candidate position evaluate a content-dependent boundary predicate (rolling hash threshold for Rabin/Gear/FastCDC-family algorithms; local-extremum/skip-based rule for AE/MAXP/RAM/SeqCDC-family algorithms) to decide whether to cut a chunk boundary there. SeqCDC's specific contribution: a lightweight (non-hash) boundary-detection rule plus content-defined SKIPPING (jumping ahead by a content-dependent stride instead of evaluating every byte position), vectorized via SSE/AVX/NEON/AltiVec to evaluate multiple candidate positions per SIMD lane-width.

variants.claim: steady-state single-thread chunking throughput on a real (non-synthetic) dataset, reported JOINTLY with achieved average chunk size and resulting deduplication space savings %, across the SIMD-acceleration axis (unaccelerated vs. best-available vector ISA for the host CPU) and the chunk-size-target axis -- matches SeqCDC's own claimed "10x over unaccelerated / 1.2-1.35x over vector-accelerated alternatives" comparison set (the other 10 algorithms in the same DedupBench harness).

convolution.summary: Forward 2D convolution (NCHW) for CNN-inference-shaped workloads, covering four legitimately different algorithm classes found in the surveyed literature — dense direct/im2col-implicit-GEMM, sparse structured-pruned, sub-8-bit/binary quantized, and autotuning-search cost — each measured with a fixed protocol so GFLOP/s numbers across algorithm classes stay comparable rather than being inflated by a smaller executed-op count.
convolution.operation: Y[N,Cout,Hout,Wout] = conv2d(X[N,Cin,Hin,Win], W[Cout,Cin/groups,Kh,Kw], stride=(Sh,Sw), pad=(Ph,Pw), groups=g); groups=1 for standard conv, groups=Cin=Cout for depthwise. Reference (algorithm-invariant) FLOP count used for the primary GFLOP/s metric in every variant: flops_ref = 2 * N * Cout * (Cin/groups) * Kh * Kw * Hout * Wout — this is the "problem size" FLOP count (same formula regardless of whether the implementation is direct, im2col-GEMM, Winograd, FFT-conv, or sparse/pruned), so an algorithm that does fewer *executed* multiply-adds (Winograd, sparse) can legitimately show GFLOP/s above the executed-op rate; that is expected and must not be hidden — see metric definitions per variant below.

variants.claim: Steady-state kernel throughput of a dense conv (direct, im2col-implicit-GEMM, Winograd, or FFT-conv — algorithm class must be disclosed), fp32, single layer, preprocessing (schedule search / weight-layout transform) excluded from timed calls and reported separately, once.

Steady-state kernel throughput of a structured/unstructured-pruned sparse conv, fp32, reported both as a same-shape apples-to-apples comparison against dense baselines run on the identical pruned shape, AND as an end-user speedup against the dense baseline run on the ORIGINAL unpruned shape (these are different questions and both are needed — see notes_on_fairness).

Steady-state kernel throughput of a sub-8-bit or binary/XNOR quantized conv, reported per (weight_bits, activation_bits) precision class; correctness is defined against a reference computation AT THE SAME PRECISION (quantization is intentionally lossy vs. fp32, so an fp32-relative tolerance is the wrong gate).

Time-to-reach-target-performance from a cold start (no cached schedule/tuning database) — a distinct, non-per-call metric that is the actual subject of Ansor-AF-DS's contribution and is implicitly claimed to be near-zero by the analytical-tiling paper (ASPLOS'21); NOT blended into the steady-state GFLOP/s of conv-dense-kernel-fp32.

dnn-operator-fusion.summary: Fusing a chain of DNN subgraph operators (elementwise / reduction / GEMM combinations pulled from attention, normalization, MoE routing, and quantized-GEMM building blocks) into as few kernel launches as legally possible, measured separately at single-fused-kernel, subgraph, and full-model granularity, with compile/autotuning search time reported as its own axis rather than hidden inside any of those three.
dnn-operator-fusion.operation: Generic: given an operator chain op1 -> op2 -> ... -> opk drawn from the canonical pattern set below, produce a fused kernel (or minimal kernel set) computing the same function as the unfused sequential execution of op1..opk, and compare launch count / latency / bandwidth against the unfused baseline and against the best available hand-written reference.

variants.claim: steady-state latency/bandwidth of ONE fused kernel in isolation (synthetic harness, decoupled from any specific model), i.e. the "single-fused-kernel" granularity that RedFuser's four subgraphs and SumMerge collapse into by construction, and that LightSeq2 reports per-operator (10 reps).

fused kernel(s) exercised inside a larger block including adjacent unfused glue ops (reshape/transpose/gather) — RedFuser's actual reporting granularity ("four representative subgraphs"), and STOF's MHA-block-in-context numbers.
full-model forward-inference and/or one full training step latency, with the fusion framework's kernels embedded in a real model, matching STOF's and LightSeq2's end-to-end tables.

compile/autotune search time for the fusion framework, reported separately and explicitly amortized, never silently folded into fusion-e2e-model latency. Mandatory for any codegen/autotuning-based entrant (RedFuser-, STOF-, MCFuser-, Bolt-style systems); reported as 0 / N-A for hand-written systems (LightSeq2-style), which is itself a valid and meaningful data point, not a missing one.

dp-dynamic-programming.summary: All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) on large sparse graphs via a hybrid dynamic program: dense Floyd-Warshall recurrence tiled within METIS-partitioned subgraphs, combined with global Dijkstra (SSSP) sweeps across subgraph boundaries, run distributed across multiple MPI ranks / GPUs, to avoid the all-to-all communication a naive blocked-Floyd-Warshall APSP requires.
dp-dynamic-programming.operation: Given a graph G=(V,E) (weighted or unweighted, directed or undirected), compute shortest-path distance (and predecessor) between every pair of vertices: d(k)[i][j] = min(d(k-1)[i][j], d(k-1)[i][k] + d(k-1)[k][j]) applied locally per METIS partition, reconciled globally via per-boundary-vertex Dijkstra sweeps across the k=1..|V| recurrence.

variants.claim: steady-state solve throughput as a function of graph size and METIS partition count K, one-shot METIS partitioning + sparse-format load excluded from solve time and reported separately, since preprocessing cost (partitioning) does not amortize the same way across problem sizes and the paper's own contribution is specifically about avoiding per-partition global communication at solve time.

solve throughput across the four structural graph-property combinations (directed x weighted) the artifact's own codebase treats as first-class cases, since the DP recurrence and the Dijkstra cross-check both behave differently on each (directed graphs require asymmetric distance matrices; unweighted graphs reduce Dijkstra to BFS-style hop counting).

dynamic-graph-kernel.summary: Maintaining or computing a query-able result R over a graph G that evolves through a sequence of timestamped edge batches, covering two distinct problem shapes this track's own papers target: (1) genuine incremental MAINTENANCE of a live result (an SSSP tree) under a stream of edge insertions/deletions, where batch size and insert/delete mix are semantic choices that affect result staleness; and (2) one-shot STREAMING ANALYTICS over an already-complete historical temporal-edge log (temporal motif counting), where "batch"/chunk size is a pure performance-tuning knob with no effect on the (single, final) answer. The two are kept as separate variant families rather than forced onto one shared metric, per notes_on_fairness.
dynamic-graph-kernel.operation: Family A (maintenance): R_i = Update(R_{i-1}, B_i) for a sequence of edge-change batches B_1..B_k (each B_i a set of (u,v,w,op) tuples, op in {insert, delete}), where R_i must be observably equivalent to Recompute(G_i) from scratch (G_i = G_0 with B_1..B_i applied), and a point query Q(R_i, s, t) = shortest-path distance/parent from s to t must be answerable after each B_i commits. Family B (streaming analytics): Count_M(G) = number of valid delta-temporal-motif matches for motif template M in a FIXED temporal edge multiset G = {(u_i,v_i,t_i)}, computed once by streaming G through memory in temporal-chunk order; G itself is never mutated during a run.

variants.claim: update-latency and post-update query-latency of a maintained SSSP result under a stream of edge insertions and deletions, swept across batch size and insert/delete mix — the direct operationalization of this track's "update batch sizes, insert/delete mix, update-throughput vs. query-latency" axes, modeled on Khanda et al.'s incremental-SSSP-maintenance problem.

aggregate streaming throughput and end-to-end completion latency for a ONE-SHOT analytics query (temporal motif counting) over a fixed, complete historical temporal-edge log, with chunk/batch size swept as a performance-tuning knob (NOT a semantic insert/delete axis — no mutation occurs in this variant) — the direct operationalization of DTMiner's own evaluation shape, kept separate from dgk-incremental-update-latency because conflating "chunk size for cache locality" with "batch size for update semantics" would misrepresent what either paper actually varies.

one-shot cost of building the initial data structure — either the SSSP rooted-tree/auxiliary-edge structure (Family A) or the chunk/hierarchical index (Family B) — from a static starting graph, reported standalone rather than folded silently into the first update or the first query, since both papers in this track build a nontrivial structure before any update/query timing begins and neither fully separates that cost from steady-state numbers in their own headline results.

eigensolver.summary: Symmetric eigenvalue decomposition spanning three claims this track's own literature treats as genuinely different: dense single-GPU full-spectrum 2-stage EVD (tridiagonalize + divide-and-conquer + back-transform, with tile size and back-transform panel width as required disclosed parameters); distributed structured divide-and-conquer for the symmetric TRIDIAGONAL full-spectrum sub-problem (with deflation threshold as a required disclosed parameter); and polynomial-filtered PARTIAL-spectrum solves (k eigenpairs inside a disclosed interval, generalized or standard eigenproblem), with the matrix-power-kernel degree and the search interval itself as required, disclosed, spec-level parameters. Every paper in this 5-paper track is symmetric or symmetric-definite-generalized; no genuinely nonsymmetric eigensolver appears in this track's literature — this spec covers the symmetric case only and flags the nonsymmetric gap explicitly (see notes_on_fairness and open_questions) rather than fabricating a variant unevidenced by any surveyed paper.
eigensolver.operation: Standard form: A[N,N] (symmetric) = Q[N,N] * Lambda[N,N] * Q[N,N]^T, Q orthogonal (Q^T*Q=I), Lambda diagonal with eigenvalues as its diagonal entries. Generalized form: A[N,N]*x = lambda*B[N,N]*x, A,B symmetric, B positive (semi)definite. FULL-spectrum variants compute all N eigenpairs (optionally with eigenvectors); PARTIAL-spectrum variants compute only the k eigenpairs whose eigenvalues fall inside a disclosed interval [lambda_lo, lambda_hi], via polynomial-filtered Krylov iteration built on a matrix-power kernel A^d*x (or a shifted/scaled operator's power) as the dominant per-iteration cost.

variants.claim: steady-state single-GPU dense symmetric EVD, full spectrum WITH eigenvectors, via the standard 2-stage pipeline (dense -> band -> tridiagonal -> tridiagonal-eigensolve -> back-transform), with BLOCK SIZE and BACK-TRANSFORM PANEL WIDTH as required, disclosed CLI parameters and a MANDATORY per-stage timing breakdown — matches WangDZWZLJZ25 (tridiagonalization) and WangHZSJWDZ25 (back- transformation)'s own combined pipeline exactly (their successor artifact, ASE, implements both papers' contributions together and is this variant's primary source). WangDZWZLJZ25's own headline finding motivates the mandatory per-stage breakdown: on cuSOLVER, FP64 tridiagonalization alone consumes "over 97%" of total EVD time — a single end-to-end number would hide exactly the bottleneck this track's own papers are about.

distributed (multi-node) structured divide-and-conquer eigensolver for the symmetric TRIDIAGONAL full-spectrum sub-problem, with DEFLATION THRESHOLD K as a required, disclosed, per-matrix-tuned parameter alongside tile size — matches LiaoLLR21 (PSDC) exactly, the one distributed paper in this track and the natural companion to variant 1's dense-to-tridiagonal reduction stage (this variant picks up exactly where variant 1's tridiagonalization stage leaves off).

PARTIAL-spectrum eigensolve (only the k eigenpairs inside a disclosed interval [lambda_lo, lambda_hi]), via polynomial-filtered Krylov iteration, with the SEARCH INTERVAL and the underlying matrix-power- kernel POLYNOMIAL DEGREE both required, disclosed, spec-level parameters — this is the one variant in this track's spec that addresses the "partial spectrum" half of the task's own key axis, combining ShiLXSH21 (the application-level generalized-eigenproblem solve, interval-bounded) with YangNYLDXJ026 (the kernel-level matrix-power-kernel optimization that makes exactly this class of solve efficient) as complementary, not merely co-located, evidence.

embedding-ops.summary: Embedding-table gather/pooling kernels as used by DLRM-style recommendation models and by single-index gather workloads (knowledge-graph embeddings, word embeddings), measured under both uniform and power-law-skewed row access, with pooling-factor/batch axes matched to production-scale tables.
embedding-ops.operation: DLRM-style pooled: Y[b, :] = Pool_{j in bag(b)}( Table[idx_j, :] )  for b in [0, batch), Pool in {sum, mean}, |bag(b)| = pooling_factor (may be per-batch variable). Single-index (KGE/W2V-style): y[b, :] = f( Table1[i1(b), :], Table2[i2(b), :], ... ) for a fused elementwise/bilinear function f (e.g. TransE: Eemb[h]-Eemb[t]+Remb[r]).

variants.claim: steady-state pooled-embedding-gather kernel throughput, index/bag construction excluded (reported separately, see embed-dlrm-e2e-preproc)
end-to-end pooled-embedding path including one-shot per-batch index/bag construction, amortized over k=128 batches (matches RecFlex examples/end_to_end.py sample_batch_nums default)

steady-state single-index (non-pooled) embedding gather + fused elementwise/bilinear op, as used by KGE and word-embedding workloads (cuKE, FULL-W2V style); preprocessing (graph/corpus loading, negative sampling) excluded

erasure-coding.summary: CPU XOR-based Reed-Solomon erasure coding (encode: compute m parity blocks from k data blocks via GF(2) XOR-schedules compiled and optimized as straight-line programs; decode: reconstruct erased blocks from surviving data+parity), measured separately for encode, decode at maximum tolerable erasure count, and degraded-read at partial erasure, across (k,m) configurations and the paper's own three-tier optimization ablation (Nooptim / Fusion / FusionSchedule).
erasure-coding.operation: Given k data blocks D_1..D_k (each BLOCK_SIZE bytes), compute m parity blocks P_1..P_m such that any k of the (k+m) total blocks suffice to reconstruct all k original data blocks, using ONLY XOR operations (no Galois-field multiplication) — i.e. each P_j and each reconstructed D_i is a fixed XOR-subset of the surviving blocks, with that XOR schedule compiled as a straight-line program (SLP) and optimized via grammar compression (fewer XOR ops), deforestation (fewer memory accesses), and pebble-game scheduling (fewer cache misses) before execution.

variants.claim: steady-state single-thread CPU throughput for encode and decode (at maximum-tolerable erasure count, i.e. exactly m blocks erased) separately, at each of the paper's own three optimization tiers, across a spread of (k,m) configurations -- SLP compilation/ optimization is a one-shot cost EXCLUDED from the per-run timed loop (matching the artifact's own code structure, which already separates estimate_compile from the timed run::run_program loop).

fdtd-seismic.summary: Throughput of explicit finite-difference-time-domain (FDTD) forward wave-propagation solvers for seismic imaging — isotropic/anisotropic acoustic and elastic wave equations discretized on a regular 3D grid with a damped absorbing-boundary layer, evaluated single-node (order-of-accuracy and temporal-blocking axes) and distributed-memory (halo-exchange-pattern and weak/strong-scaling axes), plus a lower-confidence proprietary-dataflow- hardware variant. Grounded in the Devito DSL/compiler lineage (2 papers, shared artifact with the general `stencil` track); consistent with `benchspecs/stencil/spec.yaml`'s grid-size/timing conventions where the underlying workload is literally the same code, reframed around this track's own primary axes (order of accuracy, absorbing-boundary cost, GPoints/s).
fdtd-seismic.operation: U_out[p] = FD_stencil(U_in, coefficients, space_order) applied at every interior point p of a 3D velocity-model grid for one timestep, for T sequential CFL-determined timesteps; a damped absorbing-boundary-condition (ABC) layer of width w surrounds the physical domain (grid dimension = physical_size + 2w per axis); equation family in {isotropic acoustic, anisotropic/TTI acoustic, isotropic elastic, visco-elastic} per Bisbas et al.'s 4-kernel taxonomy.

variants.claim: Steady-state single-node throughput of an FD wave-propagation kernel at a fixed space-discretization order, with the one-shot autotuning/blocking-parameter search excluded from the timed region and reported separately — the common denominator this track's two code-grounded papers (BisbasLLNGK21, BisbasNLLKG25) share, and directly comparable to `stencil` track's variant 3 (`stencil-e2e-application`) for the same underlying Devito code.

Distributed-memory (MPI-X) strong/weak-scaling throughput at fixed per-node grid size, with 3 halo-exchange communication patterns compared head-to-head — BisbasNLLKG25's own paper-native contribution and the sole confirmed source for this variant.

Half/mixed-precision or dataflow-architecture-specific FDTD throughput on proprietary hardware (Cerebras wafer-scale engine, Huawei Ascend NPU) — the LOWEST-CONFIDENCE variant in this track's spec, included for completeness because 2 of the 5 surveyed papers target this hardware class, but every field below is sourced from an abstract or an unverified web-search snippet, not a paper PDF or artifact.

fft.summary: Throughput of the (Fast) Fourier Transform — forward and inverse, complex-to-complex (C2C) and real-to-complex/complex-to-real (R2C/C2R), 1D/2D/3D, batched — across the four usage patterns this track's own papers actually benchmark: a bare batched-kernel microbenchmark (TurboFFT, TurboFNO, cuFalcon), an FFT embedded inside a larger scientific pipeline on a dense regular grid (FFCz, CLAIRE, cuHPX's ring-FFT), a distributed multi-node/multi-GPU transform whose all-to-all (or device-direct) communication dominates at scale (FLUPS, CLAIRE), and the one-shot plan-creation / kernel-codegen cost every one of those targets pays before its first transform and which none of them consistently reports as its own number (this track's analogue of "preprocessing").
fft.operation: Y = FFT_dims(X, direction), X a dense array of shape [batch, N_1, ..., N_d] (d in {1,2,3}), direction in {forward, inverse}; C2C keeps X,Y complex of the same shape, R2C/C2R halve/double the last transformed dimension per the standard Hermitian-symmetry packing. N_i may be a power of two (the majority convention in this track's own papers) or mixed-radix (FlashFFTStencil's PFA-decomposed 56/64/128, cuHPX's ellmax=3*nside-1). "Plan creation" denotes whatever one-shot setup a given implementation requires before its first transform of a given (shape, precision, direction) configuration — a runtime plan object (cufftPlan*/fftw_plan_dft*), a build-time kernel-codegen+compile step (TurboFFT/TurboFNO), or a precomputed Green's-function+communication pattern (FLUPS) — see survey.md Divergence 3.

variants.claim: Steady-state batched 1D FFT kernel throughput, power-of-two AND mixed-radix lengths, both fp32 and fp64, with plan creation / kernel codegen excluded from the timed region but measured once and reported separately (never silently amortized in). This is the common denominator across TurboFFT, TurboFNO, and cuFalcon's internal FFT use — the three papers in this track that treat FFT as (or reduce to) a bare batched-kernel call rather than a step inside a larger pipeline.

End-to-end round-trip (forward + inverse) FFT throughput on a dense 2D/3D regular grid, with ONE-SHOT plan creation amortized over k round trips (k reported explicitly) — representative of how FFT actually appears in this track's application-embedded papers (FFCz's compression-correction pass, CLAIRE's registration-solver preconditioner, cuHPX's ring-FFT-plus-Legendre-transform, FLUPS's Poisson solve) rather than as a bare kernel call.

Distributed multi-node/multi-GPU FFT weak-scaling throughput, with local transform compute time and inter-rank communication (all-to-all, non-blocking, or device-direct) time reported as TWO SEPARATE numbers rather than one conflated total — representative of FLUPS (CPU+MPI) and CLAIRE (multi-GPU+MPI), the only two papers in this track that report genuinely distributed FFT numbers.

Isolated, one-shot plan-creation / kernel-codegen / Green's-function- and-communication-pattern-setup cost, measured ALONE and reported once per configuration — never silently amortized into any other variant's per-call number. This is this track's realization of the "preprocessing" axis every other kernel track in this benchmark suite separates out, generalized to cover BOTH a classical runtime plan object (cuFFT `cufftPlan*`, FFTW `fftw_plan_dft*`) AND a build-time kernel-codegen+compile step (TurboFFT/TurboFNO's own architecture, which has NO runtime plan call at all — survey.md Divergence 3).

gemm.summary: Dense general matrix-matrix multiplication (including uniform-shape batched GEMM and small-scale distributed GEMM); quantized/int8 GEMM is explicitly out of scope (see the quantized-gemm track).
gemm.operation: C[M,N] = alpha*A[M,K]*B[K,N] + beta*C[M,N] (beta=0 unless noted); row-major storage by convention of this spec (papers surveyed used a mix of row-/column-major and NN/NT/TN/TT layouts — the harness must record which layout each measured run used, since LibShalom shows NT materially outperforms NN for some irregular shapes on the same hardware).

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput on large/near-square dense GEMM, preprocessing (allocation, JIT/codegen, autotuning search) excluded from the timed region but reported once, separately. This is the common-denominator "textbook HPC GEMM" variant most surveyed papers report in some form (WuZLHJWC23, CA3DMM's per-rank number, CL-DB-GEMM's "around 2048"/multiples-of-128 sweep, fBLAS, Tensile-FGPS/DGEMM).

steady-state kernel throughput on small and irregular (tall-skinny / long-rectangular) GEMM shapes sourced from real scientific and DNN/LLM workloads, with cache state as an explicit reported axis. This is the variant where the literature most disagrees on scope (hot vs. cold cache changes rankings by up to 2x per LibShalom), so both states are required, not one.

steady-state throughput of uniform-shape batched GEMM (same M,N,K across the batch, independent problems, no data reuse across batch elements), preprocessing excluded. Thin in the literature (only 2 of 9 surveyed papers exercise it with real numbers) but explicitly in scope per this track's definition ("dense GEMM incl. batched").

end-to-end distributed dense GEMM across multiple nodes/GPUs, including one-shot input/output data redistribution, amortized over k=10 runs (k chosen to match CA3DMM's own example CLI usage, `ntest=10`, which is the only concrete k found in this track's survey); the kernel-only "local matmul" component is also reported separately, since CA3DMM's own tool already computes this split internally.

gemv.summary: Dense and mixed/low-precision matrix-vector multiplication (including the batch=1..~32 "thin-GEMM" regime that dominates LLM autoregressive decode, and format-compressed variants where decompression cannot be factored out of the timed kernel); a fundamentally memory-bandwidth- bound operation, unlike GEMM, so GB/s and roofline fraction (not GFLOP/s) are this track's primary metric.
gemv.operation: y[M] = alpha*A[M,K]*x[K] + beta*y[M] (beta=0 unless noted); A may be full-precision (fp64/fp32/fp16) or a packed low-bit format (INT4/INT3/ INT2, optionally nonuniform-bitwidth across columns as in QIGen) paired with per-group FP16 scale/zero-point tensors, in which case "A" in the byte-accounting below means the packed representation actually read, not a hypothetical dequantized dense array. The harness must record which of these representations was measured, since bandwidth is dominated almost entirely by how A is stored, not by x or y.

variants.claim: steady-state kernel bandwidth on full-precision dense GEMV across a shape sweep spanning tall-skinny, short-fat, and square aspect ratios, with an explicit 3-state cache axis (see cache_state below) instead of a naive hot/cold binary — the common-denominator variant grounded directly in TLR-MVM's own dense-GEMV comparison harness (`benchmark/cuda/bench_mvm_cuda_fp32.cpp`), the only paper in this survey shipping a general-purpose, precision-parameterized dense-GEMV micro-benchmark rather than an application-embedded one.

steady-state kernel bandwidth for the batch=1 (single-token decode, the literal "vector" case) regime of mixed/low-precision LLM weight-matrix x FP16-activation GEMV — in scope for this track rather than split into a separate quantized-gemv track because 3 of this track's 5 input papers (QIGen, MARLIN, PackKV) are exactly this workload; unlike GEMM's quantized-gemm split (see benchspecs/gemm/spec.yaml's summary), this track's own literature is dominated by the quantized case, so keeping it here reflects what the track's papers actually do rather than a policy choice made in advance.

throughput across the batch-size sweep that crosses GEMV's memory-bound/compute-bound roofline knee — MARLIN's own central empirical claim (near-ideal 4x quantization speedup sustained up to batch ~16-32, degrading above that as the operation becomes compute-bound) is itself a benchmark-methodology finding, not just a result, so this variant makes the batch axis a first-class, always-swept dimension rather than a single fixed point.

end-to-end throughput for GEMV embedded in a compressed/structured storage format where decompression is NOT separable from the per-call kernel by the algorithm's own design (unlike this benchmark suite's usual "preprocessing excluded, reported separately" rule) — covers TLR-MVM's tile-low-rank compressed MVM and PackKV's fused decompression+GEMV, the two surveyed papers whose own methodology times decompression/decoding together with the arithmetic because there is no natural "already decoded" state to start a kernel-only clock from.

gnn-aggregation.summary: Sparse-times-dense-matrix neighbor aggregation as used in GNN message passing (C = A_sparse @ X_dense, optionally symmetrically normalized by degree), measured at three DIFFERENT scopes the surveyed literature conflates under one "SpMM"/"aggregation" label — isolated kernel, single-layer forward with real feature dims, and full training epoch — plus an explicit preprocessing-amortization split, since several artifacts' headline numbers move visibly (EPPGCN: 1.48-5.65x kernel-only vs 1.03-1.37x end-to-end) depending on which scope and preprocessing treatment is chosen.
gnn-aggregation.operation: Forward: H'[V,F] = A_hat[V,V](sparse, given CSR) @ H[V,F](dense row-major), where A_hat is either the raw binary/weighted adjacency or its symmetric degree-normalization D^-1/2 A D^-1/2 (both appear as first-class targets in the surveyed papers, e.g. CBM benchmarks all three of A@X, A@D^-1/2@X, D^-1/2@A@D^-1/2@X separately). Backward (where in scope): grad_H[V,F] = A_hat^T @ grad_H'[V,F] (same operation shape, transposed sparse operand).

variants.claim: steady-state isolated-kernel throughput of one aggregation call, given CSR (no format conversion timed), synthetic dense features swept over N — the common denominator of GE-SpMM, MaxK-GNN's kernel benchmark, TLPGNN, and CBM's benchmark_matmul.py. THIS variant intentionally does NOT include any Python/framework dispatch overhead, backward pass, or other GCN layers (unlike TC-GNN/QGTC/EPPGCN's epoch numbers below).

end-to-end throughput including one-shot preprocessing (sparse-format conversion to the kernel's native layout, e.g. CBM's compression, MaxK-GNN's CBSR meta-data generation, TC-GNN's dense-tile graph translation), amortized over k=200 repeated aggregation calls — 200 matches TC-GNN's own full-training epoch count, the most common "realistic reuse count" a GNN aggregation kernel actually sees before the graph structure would plausibly change.

one GCN-layer forward pass (aggregation immediately followed by the dense weight GEMM) on STANDARD datasets using each dataset's REAL input/hidden feature width, not a synthetic N sweep — isolates what TLPGNN/FeatGraph measure (a single aggregation call inside a real model configuration) from the raw kernel-only variant above, and reports the aggregation-kernel fraction of the layer separately from the GEMM fraction (a breakdown none of the surveyed papers isolate cleanly at this granularity).

full training-epoch time (forward + backward + optimizer step) for a standard 2-layer GCN — the headline number TC-GNN, QGTC, and the EPPGCN/GNNAdvisor lineage actually report and compare against. Kept as its own variant, explicitly labeled as NOT kernel-isolated, because most of this track's papers report exactly this number and a fair benchmark spec must let their claims be reproduced on the SAME dataset/model instead of only comparing incommensurable kernel-only numbers (see survey.md Divergence 1).

graph-layout.summary: GPU-accelerated 2D force-directed / Path-Guided Stochastic Gradient Descent (PG-SGD) layout of pangenome variation graphs, measured as wall-clock time to complete a fixed SGD iteration schedule, with layout quality (Sampled Path Stress) reported jointly with time since this is a non-convex optimization with no single correct output.
graph-layout.operation: coords[V,2] = PG_SGD(graph G=(V,E,paths), iteration_schedule, step_size_schedule); minimizes sum over sampled (path, node_i, node_j) triples of (||coords_i - coords_j|| - path_distance(i,j))^2 / path_distance(i,j)^2; output is a 2D embedding of every node.

variants.claim: steady-state layout wall time on the complete HPRC Year-1 whole-chromosome pangenome suite; graph loading (.og deserialization) excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

end-to-end time including one-shot graph loading, for the case where loading cost is non-negligible relative to layout time on smaller chromosomes (loading is NOT amortized across multiple layout calls in real pangenome-analysis usage — each chromosome is laid out once)

graph-partitioning.summary: Divide a graph's vertices into k balanced blocks while minimizing the cut (sum of edge weights crossing block boundaries), measured as wall-clock partitioning time with cut quality and achieved imbalance reported jointly — a faster partitioner that produces a worse cut, or that silently violates its own balance constraint, is not a win. The track's two papers occupy almost disjoint (k, graph-scale, hardware) regimes, so the spec keeps them as separate scale-regime variants rather than forcing a single combined leaderboard, while anchoring both to the one convention they already agree on (imbalance epsilon = 3%).
graph-partitioning.operation: P[V] = Partition(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, weighted or unweighted, undirected), k, epsilon); output is a vertex-to-block-ID assignment P: V -> {0, ..., k-1} such that (a) BALANCE: for every block p_i, weight(p_i) <= (1+epsilon) * sum(weight(V)) / k, and (b) the CUT = sum of weights of edges (u,v) with P(u) != P(v) is minimized subject to (a). k and epsilon are caller-supplied parameters (unlike the community-detection track, where the number of communities is discovered rather than specified).

variants.claim: steady-state partitioning kernel time at G-kway's operating point — small power-of-2 k, graphs in the low-tens-of-millions-of-edges range — runnable on either a single GPU or a single CPU node, so GPU- and CPU-based partitioners can be compared on shared public instances instead of on disjoint hardware as the two surveyed papers currently are

steady-state partitioning kernel time at TeraPart's operating point — wide/irregular k up to tens of thousands, graphs from hundreds of millions to trillions of edges — CPU/distributed-only, since no GPU partitioner in this track (or known to the surveyed literature) currently operates at this scale

dedicated memory-efficiency measurement at the largest (graph, k) each submitted implementation can complete within a fixed memory budget — operationalizes TeraPart's own headline contribution (16x peak-memory reduction at comparable quality/speed) as a first-class, reportable variant instead of a claim buried in a single "under 8 minutes, 900 GiB" narrative, and gives any future memory-efficiency- focused submission (in the spirit of HSSInfo in the community-detection track, though no such paper currently exists in THIS track) a variant that measures what it actually contributes

end-to-end throughput including one-shot graph loading and format/CSR construction; like community detection (and unlike BFS), graph partitioning is inherently single-shot per (graph, k) input — there is no repeated-query amortization argument — so this variant reports ONE full run's total time rather than an amortized-over-k number

graph-pattern-mining.summary: Counting (not full enumeration) the number of occurrences of a fixed, unlabeled subgraph pattern — triangles, k-cliques, 4-node motifs, and a handful of named 5-7 vertex shapes — in a large simple undirected graph, measured as steady-state search kernel time with one-shot graph preprocessing (CSR build, orientation, any auxiliary index) reported separately, never folded silently into per-pattern time.
graph-pattern-mining.operation: count(G, P) = number of distinct (up to automorphism) vertex subsets of simple undirected graph G = (V,E) that are isomorphic to pattern P; G given as CSR/edge-list, P given as a small fixed adjacency list (3-7 vertices). Full match enumeration/listing is explicitly OUT of scope for the core variants (see notes_on_fairness).

variants.claim: steady-state counting-kernel time for small patterns (3-4 vertices: the clique ladder K3-K4 plus the full 4-motif census), preprocessing excluded and reported separately — the scope every one of the 8 in-scope papers already uses for its smallest patterns (GraphFold TC, GLumin P4, cuTS/STMatch triangle-in-query-set, GraphSet motif_counting).

steady-state counting-kernel time for the harder combinatorial regime (5-7 vertex patterns: K5/K6/K7 and the named non-clique shapes), where papers diverge most in what "handles large patterns" means (Fringe-SGC's whole premise is that "current SGC approaches can only handle very small patterns because computational load increases exponentially with pattern size") — same input suite and protocol as gpm-kernel-small-f32, isolated as its own variant because DNF/timeout rates are expected to be far higher here, and that rate is itself part of what the benchmark should surface.

end-to-end time including one-shot graph preprocessing (parse+CSR build, orientation/degree-ordering, and any auxiliary index the tested system builds), amortized over k repeated pattern-counting calls on the same loaded graph — the realistic usage pattern every one of the 8 in-scope artifacts' own scripts actually exercises (each loads one graph once, then runs multiple pattern queries against it: GLumin runs {P1,P2,P5,P6} per load, GraphFold runs TC+CF4-7+MC4 per load, cuTS runs all 33 patterns per graph, VSGM runs 19 patterns + k-clique/k-motif sweeps against its single friendster load) — yet none of them state this amortization count explicitly, they just run the multi-pattern loop and report each cell's number as if preprocessing weren't shared. This variant makes the amortization count k explicit instead of leaving it implicit in a driver script.

hamiltonian-simulation.summary: Classical (non-quantum-hardware) time evolution e^{-iHt}|psi_0> of sparse quantum Hamiltonians via Trotterization, benchmarked both end-to-end (diagonal-budgeted step-count search + repeated propagator application) and as an isolated diagonal-sparse SpMV/matrix-exponential kernel, gated by state fidelity against a dense NumPy reference where memory permits (system size in {qubits}, matching the parent task's suggested axis directly -- see survey.md Divergences #4).
hamiltonian-simulation.operation: Given Hamiltonian H (sum of Pauli-string terms, read from a HamLib HDF5 file) and final time T: (1) [diaq method only, one-time preprocessing] binary/exponential-search the smallest step count r such that num_diagonals(exp(-i*H*(T/r))) <= D_max (a user-set diagonal budget); (2) compute the per-step propagator U = exp(-i*H*(T/r)) once (dense matrix exponential over the Hamiltonian's sparse/diagonal representation); (3) apply U to the initial state vector r times via repeated diagonal- sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV): psi_r = U^r psi_0.

variants.claim: end-to-end wall-clock time for full Hamiltonian time evolution (diagonal-budget step-count search, included as reported one-time preprocessing, PLUS r repeated propagator applications), across HamLib's 4 problem families and the paper's own qubit-count range, compared against 6 baselines run in the SAME driver script (fair, same-harness comparison per survey.md)

isolated diagonal-sparse SpMV kernel throughput, separating the core linear-algebra primitive from Trotter-step orchestration and HamLib I/O overhead the end-to-end variant also pays -- included because the parent task's "per-step time" axis is most directly answered by this isolated kernel, not the end-to-end application number

hash-table.summary: Concurrent/parallel hash-table performance under three distinct workload families found in this track's literature (bulk build-probe join, bulk counting/upsert, general dynamic CRUD), measured as operations per second at controlled load factor and key distribution, with memory overhead reported as a function of load factor rather than left implicit.
hash-table.operation: table[K] -> V; open-addressing (linear probing) or equivalent collision scheme; K, V fixed-width (integer or fixed-length byte string) unless a variant states otherwise; concurrent multi-threaded or single-GPU-kernel access as specified per variant.

variants.claim: steady-state GPU build+probe throughput for a static, rebuilt-per-call hash table (join-style usage: bulk insert once, then bulk lookup), no delete path, preprocessing (relation generation/H2D transfer) excluded but reported separately

steady-state throughput of a fixed-capacity counting/aggregation hash table under bulk find-or-increment-or-insert operations (the DEDUKT k-mer-counting workload shape), isolated from any surrounding communication/partitioning phase, which is reported separately

concurrent throughput of a general-purpose, dynamically-resizable hash table under configurable read/insert/update/delete ratios, following the YCSB load+run-phase convention that is this track's only literature precedent for a full CRUD op mix

hausdorff-distance.summary: Hausdorff Distance (HD) between two point sets, computed via GPU ray-tracing-core-accelerated k-NN search with spatial-grid and provably-exact branch-and-bound pruning (X-HD), measured against an exact brute-force reference and an industrial-standard baseline (ITK), across three structurally different point-set domains the artifact treats as first-class (medical imaging, geospatial, 3D graphics).
hausdorff-distance.operation: HD(A,B) = max(h(A,B), h(B,A)); h(A,B) = max_{a in A} min_{b in B} dist(a,b); A, B are point sets in R^n_dims (n_dims in {2,3}). X-HD reformulates the inner min_{b in B} dist(a,b) as an RT-accelerated k-NN query, adding a spatial grid (reduce BVH traversal intensity), HD estimators (provably-exact early-termination bounds on the running max-min), and CUDA-kernel offload of distance computation from RT shaders to fix a grid-induced load-imbalance.
