variants.claim: steady-state kernel time to compute the EXACT Hausdorff distance for a point-set pair, across four algorithm choices exposed directly by the artifact's own CLI (-variant eb/nn/itk/rt) and an execution-target axis (-execution cpu/gpu, GPU-only for rt); eb is treated as this benchmark's ground-truth reference, matching the artifact's own apparent design (see survey.md)

end-to-end throughput including one-shot index construction (BVH for nn/rt, spatial grid for rt specifically) amortized over k=10 point-set-pair queries against the same reference structure -- relevant when one point set (e.g. a fixed reference mesh/anatomical atlas) is queried against many others, a realistic batch-scoring usage this track's single-pair kernel variant does not capture

homotopy-continuation.summary: Throughput of GPU homotopy-continuation path tracking for polynomial systems, separated into a fixed-work kernel measure (all paths tracked, so efficiency gains cannot be confused with work reduction) and an application-level RANSAC measure where solution quality gates the time.
homotopy-continuation.operation: Given a polynomial system F(x; p_target) = 0 with n unknowns and a start system G(x; p_start) = 0 with known solutions, track T homotopy paths H(x, t) = (1-t) G + t F from t=0 to t=1 by predictor-corrector stepping, yielding candidate solutions of F. For trifocal_2op1p_30x30: n = 30 variables, 33 parameters, T = 312 paths.

variants.claim: path-tracking kernel efficiency at FIXED work — every path tracked to completion, pruning and early termination disabled — so that implementation speed is measured rather than algorithmic work reduction

end-to-end pose-estimation latency with pruning and early termination enabled — the configuration a SLAM/VO system deploys — with pose accuracy reported jointly so that work reduction cannot be cashed in as speed
attribution of a speedup to work reduction versus kernel efficiency, which a single wall-clock ratio cannot distinguish

json-parsing.summary: Fully GPU-offloaded JSON parsing (UTF-8 validation, tokenization, nesting-structure/structural-index recognition) measured as throughput over standard JSON corpora, covering both a single large deeply-nested document and many independent JSON-Lines records with an explicit chunking-strategy axis, with RFC 8259 validation strictness reported as a first-class disclosure alongside speed.
json-parsing.operation: Given a raw JSON byte buffer of size N: produce a structural index — for every structural character (`{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `:`, `,`, string quotes), its byte offset, plus a `pair_pos` array mapping every opening bracket/brace to its matching closer — sufficient to support O(1)-ish key/array-index navigation via a query iterator without a full recursive-descent re-parse. Standard-JSON mode processes one such buffer as a single document; JSON-Lines mode processes C independent single-object buffers (one per line), optionally pre-split into K chunks for coarse-grained parallel dispatch.

variants.claim: steady-state GPU parsing throughput (GB/s) for the full 3-phase pipeline (UTF-8 validate + tokenize + nesting-recognition) as one measured region, H2D input transfer and D2H structural-index transfer EXCLUDED and reported separately (device-resident timing is the meaningful number for a GPU-resident downstream-query pipeline; a candidate that must round-trip to host per query is a different, worse-case claim that should be reported as a distinct number, not silently substituted).

kcore-kclique.summary: Five variants covering the k-core/k-clique graph-kernel family on large simple undirected graphs: static full k-core decomposition via parallel peeling, batch-dynamic k-core maintenance under a stream of edge updates, exact k-clique counting via GPU-specialized search/orientation, approximate probabilistic clique/triangle counting via Bloom-filter/MinHash sketches, and maximal clique enumeration via GPU search-tree exploration. These are 4 distinct kernel PROBLEMS sharing only the k-core/k-clique graph-theory family, not 1 problem with 4 knobs — see notes_on_fairness for why this spec has 5 variants instead of the usual 1-4.
kcore-kclique.operation: Multi-kernel track; each variant below has its own operation definition. Common thread: given a static (or dynamically updated) simple undirected graph G=(V,E) in CSR/adjacency-list form, either (a) compute coreness(v) for every v in V (k-core decomposition, static or maintained under updates), (b) count or enumerate cliques of size k (or all maximal cliques) in G.

variants.claim: steady-state full k-core decomposition (per-vertex coreness for ALL cores simultaneously) on a static simple undirected graph via parallel peeling, one-shot preprocessing (CSR build / degree-degeneracy orientation) excluded from the kernel timer and reported separately — the common denominator across LiuSZ24's static EKCore/AKCore baselines and KCGPU's degeneracy-only peeling.

batch-dynamic k-core maintenance under a stream of edge insertions/deletions (and 50/50 mixed batches), reporting per-batch update latency — the realistic streaming-graph usage LiuSZ24's PLDS/LDS target, with a fundamentally different cost model (amortized per-batch latency, not one-shot wall time) than kcore-static-peel, so kept as a fully separate variant rather than a protocol knob.

exact k-clique counting on a static simple graph via GPU-specialized search/orientation (degree- or degeneracy-DAG orientation followed by warp-partitioned pivoting or per-node/per-edge enumeration), k swept over a fixed ladder, one-shot DAG-orientation preprocessing excluded from the kernel timer by default (KCGPU's own paper folds it in — flagged as a divergence, see notes_on_fairness).

approximate triangle- and 4-clique counting via probabilistic set representations (Bloom-filter AND-based or MinHash neighborhood- intersection estimators), trading a bounded, EXPLICITLY-REPORTED accuracy loss for CPU-parallel speedup vs. tuned exact baselines — a fundamentally different claim from kclique-count-exact and requires accuracy as a first-class reported axis, not a pass/fail gate.

exhaustive maximal clique enumeration (ALL maximal cliques, an unbounded-output problem) on a static simple graph via GPU search-tree exploration with dynamic load balancing — architecturally distinct from kclique-count-exact (bounded combinatorial count): output size is itself a first-class, unpredictable quantity, and "did it finish at all" is as important a result as the time when it does.

knn-graph-construction.summary: Distributed-memory construction of an approximate k-nearest-neighbor graph (KNNG) over high-dimensional points via a forest of sparse random projection trees (build + query), measured as construction throughput jointly with recall against an exact brute-force KNNG, since this is an approximate algorithm and speed alone is not a legitimate win.
knn-graph-construction.operation: KNNG[N,k] = ApproxKNN(X[N,D] point set, ntrees T, target_neighbors k, locality_mode); builds T sparse random-projection trees over X (each a recursive space partition via random sparse hyperplane projections), then queries the forest per point to emit its k approximate nearest neighbors as a directed graph.

variants.claim: steady-state single-node build+query throughput on standard ANN-benchmark-style point sets, at a fixed accuracy operating point; the common denominator most ANN/KNNG papers report on before addressing distributed scaling

distributed-memory strong-scaling throughput of the SAME accuracy operating point as knng-kernel-single-node, since this track's paper's central contribution is scaling KNNG construction to thousands of MPI processes on a supercomputer via a communication- reduction (locality-based data-gathering) scheme

lattice-boltzmann.summary: Throughput of an iterative lattice-Boltzmann (LBM) collision-streaming sweep over a 3D lattice, across the two workload classes this track's papers actually target: a regular cuboid domain (optionally with nested-grid spatial/temporal refinement), and a sparse/complex-geometry domain where indirect boundary/solid-fraction addressing dominates cost. Grounded in one code-verified paper (MahmoudSM24 / Autodesk XLB); the other 4 surveyed papers are abstract-only (see survey.md's Scope note — this track has NO automated-pipeline-detected artifact; MahmoudSM24's artifact was found by this survey's own manual search and corrects the pipeline's record).
lattice-boltzmann.operation: For every lattice site x and every discrete velocity direction i in the chosen velocity set (D2Q9 in 2D; D3Q19 or D3Q27 in 3D): collide f_i(x) -> f_i*(x) via a collision operator (BGK single-relaxation-time or KBC), then stream f_i*(x) -> f_i(x + e_i) along direction i's lattice vector; solid/boundary sites additionally apply a bounce-back or equilibrium boundary condition. One sweep = one collide+stream pass over every lattice site, repeated for T timesteps.

variants.claim: Steady-state per-timestep throughput of collide-stream on a regular cuboid lattice, with or without nested-grid spatial/temporal refinement, at a fixed lattice model/precision/collision-model combination — the common denominator any regular-domain LBM implementation can be measured against. Grounded directly in `Autodesk/XLB`'s `examples/performance/mlups_3d.py` (single-resolution) and `mlups_3d_multires.py` (nested-refinement) benchmark scripts.

Throughput of collide-stream on a sparse/complex-geometry domain (porous media, vascular/arterial networks, arbitrary solid boundaries), where indirect geometric addressing dominates cost — the workload class 3 of this track's 5 surveyed papers independently target (Herschlag, Gounley, Qin), none of which have a public artifact. THIS VARIANT IS LITERATURE-DERIVED, NOT CODE-VERIFIED — every field below is inferred from paper abstracts plus this track's variant-1 protocol, not confirmed against any of these 3 papers' own (unavailable) run scripts. Treat as a lower-confidence spec than variant 1.

End-to-end distributed-memory throughput/scaling for extreme-scale LBM CFD (SunwayLB's own framing) — reported separately from, never substituted for, a single-node kernel-only number from variant 1/2, matching this whole cross-track survey's standard split between kernel-only and end-to-end application variants.

lca-bridge-finding.summary: GPU adaptation of the Euler-tour technique for two exact tree/graph problems, benchmarked separately: lowest common ancestor (LCA) batch queries on trees, and bridge-finding on undirected graphs; measured as wall time across a size/shape parameter sweep, with theoretically optimal Euler-tour methods compared against simpler heuristics on both adversarial (deep/bushy) and typical (shallow) synthetic instances.
lca-bridge-finding.operation: (LCA) answer[q] = LCA(T=(V,E) tree, query batch Q subset of V x V); (bridges) isBridge[E] = Bridges(G=(V,E) undirected graph); both are unweighted, exact combinatorial problems (no approximation ratio applies to either).

variants.claim: steady-state batch-LCA-query wall time on synthetic trees, swept across size, tree-shape ("grasp"), and query-batch-size parameters, separately from ground-truth generation which is one-shot and excluded from timing

steady-state bridge-finding wall time on undirected graphs, averaged over a user-set repeat count — kept as its OWN variant (rather than merged with the LCA variant above) because the paper's own bridges harness uses mean-of-repeats rather than LCA's median-of-seeded-instances convention, and its correctness-check wiring is documented in the paper's own script as incomplete ("TODO do we want to have some tests to check correctness?")

lossless-compression.summary: Measure bit-exact lossless compression/decompression of byte and multi-byte integer streams across three distinct data domains this track's papers actually target -- generic byte-stream/text/genomic corpora, HPC/scientific multi-byte integer data (mostly SZ/cuSZ quantization-code streams and sensor/detector data), and structured LLM-weight-tensor operands feeding a downstream GEMM kernel -- reporting compression ratio and compress/decompress throughput (GB/s) jointly, never one alone, gated by a hard bit-exact roundtrip check.
lossless-compression.operation: compress: C = Compress(D) where D is a byte or multi-byte-integer stream (or, for variant 3, a structured 2D weight tensor); decompress: D' = Decompress(C); correctness requires D' == D bit-for-bit for every byte, not a statistical or average tolerance -- unlike the lossy-compression track, there is no error bound to trade off against ratio/throughput.

variants.claim: steady-state, multi-core CPU decompression throughput of standard gzip/DEFLATE-format byte streams, scaled across a fixed 3-corpus suite spanning generic text, genomic, and near-incompressible control data. The corpus's own compression ratio is treated as a FIXED, once-measured property of a reference encoder run -- never re-measured per decompressor tool -- because the one paper defining this sub-domain (Rapidgzip) is decompression-only and has no compression path of its own to time.

GPU compress/decompress kernel throughput on multi-byte scientific and sensor integer data -- mostly SZ/cuSZ intermediate quantization-code streams plus native detector data -- reported at TWO explicit scopes (kernel-only vs. full-pipeline-incl-H2D/D2H) so the two incompatible "end-to-end" meanings already identified in the lossy-compression track (GPULZ's coarse CLI wall-clock default vs. the Huffman-decoder paper's kernel-only convention) are never silently conflated. Block/ chunk/window parameters are explicitly disclosed and swept, not fixed, since GPULZ's own Table 2 shows throughput varying by >2x across its block-size grid alone.

fused decompress+downstream-compute (decompress-GEMM) kernel throughput for lossless-compressed LLM weight tensors vs. a dense uncompressed baseline kernel, gated by a standalone bit-exact weight-roundtrip check that is STRICTLY STRONGER than the correctness verification found in the one source paper's (ZipServ) own public artifact, which checks only downstream GEMM-output similarity and never the decompressed weight tensor itself.

lossy-compression.summary: Measure error-bounded lossy compression/decompression of scientific floating-point data on SDRBench-standard fields: compression ratio and throughput (GB/s) at fixed error bounds, plus a rate-distortion (PSNR-vs-bitrate) curve that lets error-bound-target (SZ-family) and rate-target (ZFP/SPERR-family) compressors be plotted on one axis.
lossy-compression.operation: compress: C = Compress(D, eb) where D is an n-dimensional fp32/fp64 array and eb is an error-bound spec (mode in {abs, rel}, value in R+); decompress: D' = Decompress(C); correctness requires max_i |D_i - D'_i| <= eb (abs mode) or <= eb * (max(D) - min(D)) (rel mode) for every element, not just on average.

variants.claim: steady-state CPU compress/decompress throughput and ratio at a fixed error bound; I/O and any one-shot autotuning search excluded and reported separately. The common denominator across the SZ-family papers (PFPL, QoZ, FAZ, TAC/TAC+, and as an SZ3-baseline reference for SPERR).

GPU kernel throughput reported at TWO explicit scopes so the two incompatible community meanings of "end-to-end" (FZ-GPU/TAC's incl.-PCIe-transfer sense vs. cuSZp's fused-single-kernel-only sense) are never conflated: (a) device-resident kernel-only throughput, and (b) full pipeline throughput including H2D input transfer and D2H compressed/decompressed output transfer.

rate-distortion curve (PSNR in dB vs. bits-per-value) comparing rate-target compressors (ZFP, SPERR) against error-bound-target compressors (SZ-family, cuSZp, FZ-GPU) on one shared axis -- resolves the track's core divergence that these two compressor families expose opposite control knobs (SPERR/ZFP take bpp as input and report resulting PSNR; SZ-family take error bound as input and report resulting bpp+PSNR).

lu.summary: Dense tile LU factorization of a general (non-symmetric) matrix, spanning three claims this track's own literature treats as genuinely different: single-node/single-GPU blocked LU with the pivoting strategy itself (partial / tournament / none) as a required, disclosed parameter; distributed communication-optimal LU built on 2.5D tournament pivoting; and extreme-scale mixed-precision (FP16/FP32 factorization + FP64 iterative-refinement correction) no-pivoting LU in the HPL-AI benchmark family. Unlike Cholesky, LU's pivoting choice is not a minor implementation detail — it changes both asymptotic communication cost and the numerical safety argument, and none of this track's own papers report a growth factor despite pivoting strategy being exactly what growth factor is designed to diagnose.
lu.operation: A[N,N] (general, non-symmetric) = P[N,N] * L[N,N] * U[N,N], tile-blocked (block size NB, tile count N/NB per dimension), where P is a permutation determined by the run's pivoting strategy: partial pivoting (row-swap, LAPACK/ScaLAPACK-style, P re-derived at every column), tournament pivoting (block-recursive candidate-pivot selection via a butterfly/playoff reduction, P propagated as row-mask indices rather than physical swaps), or no pivoting (P = I, correctness relies on the input matrix being engineered well-conditioned and/or on post-hoc iterative-refinement correction rather than on P). Mixed-precision variants additionally cast the factorization to FP16/FP32 and correct the result to FP64 accuracy via iterative refinement (IR): r = b - A*x̃ (FP64), Ad̃ = r solved via the existing FP32/FP16 L,U factors, x̃ <- x̃ + d̃, repeated to convergence.

variants.claim: steady-state single-node (shared-memory or single-GPU) dense/blocked LU factorization time, with PIVOTING STRATEGY (partial / tournament / none) as a required, per-run-disclosed parameter alongside tile size — the central lesson of this track: KwasniewskiKBZS21's own baselines (MKL, SLATE) use partial pivoting while its own COnfLUX uses tournament pivoting, and MunksgaardHSO22's Rodinia-derived LUD case study uses no pivoting at all, relying instead on a specially-constructed well-conditioned input matrix. Reporting a bare GFLOP/s number without the pivoting strategy that produced it is the LU-specific analogue of Cholesky's undisclosed-tile-size problem (see cholesky/spec.yaml notes_on_fairness) and is treated with the same required-disclosure rule here.

distributed (multi-node) dense tile LU at scale using 2.5D communication-optimal tournament pivoting, reporting time-to-solution, aggregate communication volume, AND the extra communication/ computation cost pivoting itself imposes (separable from the rest of the factorization per KwasniewskiKBZS21's own Table 1 cost model) — this is the variant KwasniewskiKBZS21's COnfLUX is purpose-built for, directly paired with cholesky-dense-distributed-fp64 (same paper, same 2.5D decomposition, same artifact repo) but with pivoting as LU's one genuinely extra axis over Cholesky.

extreme-scale mixed-precision (FP16 GEMM / FP32 panel-TRSM) no-pivot LU factorization, corrected to FP64 accuracy via iterative refinement (IR) rather than by pivoting — the HPL-AI benchmark family (LuMOEJW22's OpenMxP), a genuinely different claim from either pivoted-LU variant above: correctness here is a POST-HOC convergence property of the IR loop, not an a-priori pivoting-derived bound, and the metric convention (GFLOPS/GCD, EFLOPS at scale) and precision recipe (three distinct precisions, named per algorithmic stage) have no analogue in the other two variants.

math-functions.summary: Vectorized elementary-math-function (libm) throughput — trig, inverse-trig, exp, log, pow, fmod — for SIMD-vectorized C libraries, benchmarked across accuracy classes (1.0-ULP vs 3.5-ULP) because accuracy trades directly against speed and is treated here as a first-class axis, not an afterthought; SLEEF is the sole surveyed paper in this singleton track.
math-functions.operation: y[i] = f(x[i]) elementwise, f in {sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, exp, log, pow, fmod}, computed on a SIMD vector register of width W lanes (W = ISA vector width / element size), argument reused across a long call loop (register-resident microbenchmark, not a streaming array kernel — see notes_on_fairness).

variants.claim: Steady-state reciprocal-throughput per element for a fixed (function, accuracy class, ISA width, dtype), argument swept over SLEEF's own per-function domain buckets, correctness gated by max-ULP-error against an arbitrary-precision reference at the accuracy class's own target ULP bound.

matrix-function-evaluation.summary: Approximate evaluation of a matrix function (density-matrix sign function via Löwdin symmetric orthogonalization) on large sparse matrices from DFT electronic-structure calculations, by converting the global sparse operation into independent local dense submatrix computations that exploit CPU/GPU/FPGA dense floating-point throughput; single surveyed paper (submatrix method for CP2K, SC'20).
matrix-function-evaluation.operation: Given a sparse symmetric matrix H (Hamiltonian/overlap-type, from a CP2K DFT calculation), compute an approximation to f(H) — here the density matrix sign function — by extracting many small, nearly-dense submatrices (one per matrix row/block, up to a fixed truncation threshold eps_filter), evaluating the dense matrix function locally on each, and reassembling the sparse result. Distributed across MPI ranks; the local dense evaluation step is additionally accelerable on GPU (tensor cores) or FPGA.

variants.claim: Steady-state throughput (TFLOP/s and wall time) of the per-submatrix dense matrix-function evaluation kernel across CPU/GPU/FPGA targets, gated by an eps_filter accuracy sweep against a high-precision reference, with the sparse-to-submatrix extraction step reported separately as preprocessing rather than folded into per-call time.

maximal-independent-set.summary: Single-node multi-GPU maximal independent set (MIS) computation on undirected graphs too large for one GPU's memory, measured as steady-state throughput (Mnodes/s, Medges/s) jointly with MIS cardinality (since MIS is not unique and a smaller/degenerate output would be a false win); graph load and untimed verification excluded from per-run time.
maximal-independent-set.operation: status[V] in {in, out} = MIS(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR, undirected, binary CSR/.egr), num_gpus); a valid MIS satisfies: no two adjacent vertices are both 'in', and every 'out' vertex has at least one 'in' neighbor. A is unweighted; only connectivity matters.

variants.claim: steady-state multi-GPU MIS throughput on synthetic Graph500 R-MAT graphs sized to deliberately exceed a single GPU's memory (the exact regime MG-MIS targets); graph generation, dedup, and CSR construction excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

head-to-head comparison against the paper's own baseline (same lab's single-GPU MIS kernel run with CUDA UVM) on graphs that fit only via UVM oversubscription on 1 GPU but fit natively across the multi-GPU aggregate — this IS the paper's central claim (17.73x / 22.88x geomean speedup), elevated to its own variant since it requires a matched baseline build rather than being a standalone MG-MIS number

md-force.summary: Per-timestep short-range (and, for MLIP/ReaxFF, learned/reactive) pairwise force and potential-energy evaluation in classical molecular dynamics, including the neighbor/cell-list construction that feeds it.
md-force.operation: Given atom positions X[N,3], box/PBC, a cutoff r_c and a potential (LJ / EAM / Tersoff+ILP / ReaxFF+QEq / MLIP neural potential), compute per-atom forces F[N,3] and total potential energy E for one MD step; periodically (every k_nb steps) rebuild the neighbor/cell list used to restrict the O(N) pairwise search to r < r_c + skin.

variants.claim: steady-state force-kernel throughput for classical empirical potentials on the de facto standard LAMMPS input suite; neighbor-list build reported separately (see md-force-neighbor-list-build), not amortized into this number.

steady-state force-kernel throughput for machine-learned interatomic potentials (DeePMD-kit / TensorMD-style), which are 100-1000x more compute-intensive per atom-step than the classical potentials above and so must not be pooled with them (see Divergences).

isolated neighbor/cell-list construction throughput, reported separately because it is the axis every "rebuild every k steps" design choice in the survey trades against, and because it was 2 of the surveyed papers' actual optimization target (LMFF's SWLMFF cell list, the ReaxFF Sunway neighbor-list redesign) yet none of them isolate its cost from the force kernel in a reusable way.

end-to-end, multi-node weak-scaling throughput including amortized neighbor-list rebuild — the "Gordon-Bell-class" claim every SC paper in the survey actually reports, made comparable by fixing the metric to atom-steps/s (not ns/day, whose per-paper timestep-size confound is documented in Divergences) and requiring the timestep and rebuild interval to be stated alongside it.

membership-filter.summary: GPU approximate-membership-query (AMQ) filter data structures (GQF, TCF, RSQF, SQF, Bloom, Blocked Bloom) benchmarked for insert/query/ delete throughput, with false-positive rate reported as a MANDATORY joint measurement alongside every throughput number (never speed alone), swept across filter capacity and across uniform vs. skewed key-frequency distributions.
membership-filter.operation: A filter F of target capacity N and target false-positive rate epsilon supports: insert(key) -> void (adds key to F, using B bits/key of storage, B a function of epsilon and the filter's design); query(key) -> bool (returns true if key was inserted -- REQUIRED, zero false negatives -- or, for a key never inserted, returns true with probability <= epsilon, a false positive); delete(key) -> void, where supported (GQF, SQF, TCF only -- Bloom/Blocked-Bloom/RSQF as specified here do not support delete).

variants.claim: steady-state GPU throughput for insert, positive query, and random/false-positive query, reported JOINTLY with the empirically measured false-positive rate at each capacity -- the common denominator across all six filter types this artifact implements, matching the artifact's own point-test range (2^22 to 2^30 items).

mixed-precision-solver.summary: Solvers (dense LU, nested sparse Krylov, tile-based Cholesky) that trade numerical precision (fp8/fp16/fp32) for throughput and rely on a precision-recovery mechanism — fp64 iterative refinement, an independent fp64 residual re-check, an outer statistical-accuracy metric, or a one-shot adaptive per-tile precision choice — to reach an accuracy target this spec treats as a FIRST-CLASS, load-bearing requirement: a mixed-precision run that is fast but does not reach fp64-equivalent accuracy (or an explicitly-defined statistical/application accuracy bar) reports no valid speedup number, full stop. Four variants, one per surveyed paper's own precision-recovery strategy, since (per survey.md's Divergences) none of the four strategies reduces to any other.
mixed-precision-solver.operation: solve a linear system or covariance-parameter estimation problem using a reduced-precision computational core (fp16/fp32 factorization or fp16 inner Krylov iterations or fp8/fp16/fp32/fp64 adaptive tile precision), paired with an accuracy-recovery step (fp64 IR / independent residual recompute / outer MLE optimization / one-shot precision selection) and, where the paper's own codebase supports it, a same-codebase pure-fp64 sibling binary run on the identical input as the baseline.

variants.claim: dense LU factorization (fp32 panel decomposition + fp16 tensor-core GEMM) followed by fp64 iterative refinement to the OFFICIAL HPL-AI accuracy criterion (hplerror < 16, the same constant HPL-AI submissions use), capped at 50 refinement iterations — targets OpenMxP's exact HPL-AI benchmark design. This spec adds one mandatory fix: a run whose IR loop exhausts 50 iterations without reaching hplerror < 16 MUST be reported as a hard FAIL, not silently printed alongside converged runs — OpenMxP's own main.cpp currently prints the loop's {-1,-1} non-convergence sentinel unconditionally (residual=-1, hpl-harness=-1) with no check before the headline TFlop/s line, indistinguishable in the console output from a legitimately converged run.

nested FGMRES/Richardson Krylov cascade (fp64 outer / fp32 mid / fp16 inner) with TWO independent residual channels tracked per run (recurrence-tracked "implicit" + independently recomputed "explicit"), run back-to-back against a SAME-SCRIPT, SAME-MATRIX pure-precision baseline family (cg64/cg32/cg16, gm64/gm32/gm16) — targets F3R's exact design and its own reproduction script's paired-comparison structure, the strongest same-codebase fp64-baseline pairing found in this track.

mixed single/double-precision tile Cholesky factorization, called once per likelihood evaluation inside an outer NLopt (derivative-free) maximum-likelihood optimization loop — targets ExaGeoStat's exact MLE design. "Convergence" here is the OUTER OPTIMIZER's convergence (function-evaluation budget), not a Krylov/refinement iteration count; "accuracy" is STATISTICAL prediction quality (mean-square prediction error against held-out observations, or parameter-recovery error against known synthetic ground truth), not a floating-point residual — the mixed-precision (sdmle) run's accuracy must not degrade materially relative to the SAME-CODEBASE pure-double (dmle) run on the identical dataset/seed for the speedup to be legitimate.

one-shot (no iterative refinement, no outer optimization loop) mixed-precision tile factorization pipeline: forward spherical- harmonic transform (SHT) -> SYRK -> Cholesky factorization (adaptive per-tile precision among double/single/half/fp8, chosen ONCE before factorization, never corrected afterward) -> inverse SHT — targets hicma-x's exact climate-emulator design, the fourth and structurally most different precision-recovery strategy in this track (accuracy measured as an application-domain RMSE against a reference field, not a floating-point residual and not a statistical prediction metric).

moe-kernel.summary: Fused mixed-precision Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) FFN kernel for LLM inference: token-to-expert routing/permutation + per-expert grouped GEMM with a quantized weight operand + gate-weighted un-permute/combine, measured at steady state with routing/permutation cost reported separately, swept across expert-count/top-k configurations and both uniform and realistically-skewed token-to-expert load.
moe-kernel.operation: For a token batch X[T,H] and router logits producing top-k expert assignment per token: Y[T,H] = sum_{e in topk(t)} gate[t,e] * (X[t,:] @ W1_e[H,I] -> activation -> @ W2_e[I,H]), where W1_e/W2_e are per-expert weight matrices stored in a low-precision format (e.g. INT4/AWQ or FP8, "mixed-type" in Hexcute's own terminology) and X is bf16/fp16. Routing requires building a per-expert token permutation (gather tokens assigned to each expert into contiguous grouped-GEMM operand blocks) and an inverse permutation + gate-weighted combine on the output.

variants.claim: steady-state fused/grouped-GEMM MoE-FFN kernel throughput at fixed GPU clock, matching Hexcute's own "mixed-type MoE operator" claim (6.46x vs Triton) — token routing/permutation excluded from the timed kernel region and reported separately, since the paper itself keeps this kernel-level number distinct from its end-to-end vLLM serving numbers.

end-to-end LLM-serving throughput with the MoE kernel embedded in a real inference stack (vLLM), including router/dispatch, KV-cache, and non-MoE layers -- matches Hexcute's own reported 2.60x speedup on DeepSeek-R1-AWQ and 2.04x on a Mamba-based model. NOT kernel-isolated; kept as a separate variant precisely so it is never compared directly against moe-grouped-gemm-kernel's kernel-only number (the same fairness fix `benchspecs/quantized-gemm` applies to MixQ's end-to-end decode-loop number vs MARLIN/Tilus's kernel-only numbers).

morphology-image-kernel.summary: Generated-code throughput for an image-processing pipeline (Harris corner detector: grayscale -> Sobel gradients -> structure-tensor sum -> corner response) on mobile ARM CPUs, comparing a domain-extensible rewrite-rule compiler (Rise/Shine, and Lift) against Halide (default schedule) and OpenCV, with a mandatory per-pixel-error + PSNR correctness gate before any timing counts.
morphology-image-kernel.operation: Given an RGB image, compute the Harris corner-response map: convert to grayscale, compute Sobel x/y gradients, form the local structure tensor via a windowed (3x3) weighted sum of gradient products, and compute the corner response R = det(M) - k*trace(M)^2 (k=0.04) per pixel.

variants.claim: steady-state per-image kernel throughput across implementations and target CPUs, matching the artifact's own confirmed protocol (30 timing iterations, median/min/max), with the timer-mechanism asymmetry between implementations (wall-clock vs. OpenCL device-side events) explicitly reported rather than hidden, since it is a real methodological difference found in the source.

mst.summary: Computing a minimum spanning tree/forest (MST/MSF) of a weighted undirected graph, measured as steady-state throughput on a fixed real graph suite (aligned with benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's suite where overlap exists) at the single-node/single-GPU scale, as a distributed weak/strong-scaling curve at cluster scale, and — because this track's two papers between them demonstrate that weight distribution and tie-density materially change which algorithm family wins — as a dedicated weight-distribution sweep. Total-weight verification is a mandatory correctness gate in every variant, not an opt-in flag.
mst.operation: MST(or MSF)[|V|-1 edges] = argmin_{T subseteq E, T spans G} sum(w(e) for e in T); G = (V, E, w) undirected, w: E -> weight domain (see weight_distribution below); MSF generalizes to graphs with multiple connected components (one tree per component).

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput on named real-world graphs at the single-node/single-GPU scale (0.4M-180M edges), format given/loaded once, preprocessing excluded from the per-call number but measured and reported separately — the common-denominator claim ECL-MST's own evaluation makes directly, extended with a handful of graphs from benchspecs/bfs/spec.yaml's suite that neither MST paper used, so the two tracks' graph-suite overlap is explicit rather than coincidental.

weak- and strong-scaling throughput at distributed-cluster scale (up to tens of thousands of cores) on parameterized synthetic generator families, matching KaMSTa's own evaluation shape exactly since it is the only paper in this track's evaluation at this scale — kept as a fully separate variant from mst-kernel-real-graphs rather than trying to force one Mega-edges/s number to span both a single GPU and a 65,536-core cluster.

the dedicated, explicit weight-distribution sweep this track's brief asks for as a first-class axis — motivated directly by ECL-MST's own 99-random-seed study (Section 5.4), which shows up to ~4x throughput variance on high-average-degree scale-free graphs depending purely on which 20 sample edges happen to be picked for its filter threshold, i.e. this track's own literature already demonstrates weight/threshold randomness is NOT a negligible axis, yet neither paper reports it as a swept, first-class benchmark dimension in its own headline numbers.

mttkrp.summary: Matricized-Tensor-Times-Khatri-Rao-Product, the dominant kernel in CP-ALS tensor decomposition (and, via S3TTMc/S3TTMcTC, the closely related symmetric Tensor-Times-Matrix-chain kernel used in Tucker/HOOI/HOQRI). Given an N-mode sparse tensor X and N-1 dense factor matrices, compute the mode-n unfolding of X contracted against the Khatri-Rao product of the other factor matrices.
mttkrp.operation: M = X_(n) * (A^(N) ⊙ ... ⊙ A^(n+1) ⊙ A^(n-1) ⊙ ... ⊙ A^(1)) where X is an N-mode sparse tensor (given in some sparse format), A^(i) are dense I_i x R factor matrices, ⊙ is the Khatri-Rao (column-wise Kronecker) product, and M is the dense I_n x R result. In practice M is computed directly from the nonzeros of X (no explicit Khatri-Rao materialization).

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput on general (asymmetric) real-world sparse tensors, all modes reported, preprocessing/format-conversion excluded and reported separately once

end-to-end throughput including one-shot preprocessing (sparse-format construction and, for learned/autotuned systems, the format+schedule search), amortized over k=100 CP-ALS-style MTTKRP calls -- k chosen as a representative CP-ALS/HOOI iteration count (SySTeC/SymProp/BLCO papers all run decomposition loops in the tens-to-low-hundreds of iterations before convergence)

steady-state kernel throughput exploiting full input symmetry (all N modes are mathematically equivalent, so only one canonical-mode MTTKRP needs to be computed) on synthetic and hypergraph-derived symmetric sparse tensors

multigrid.summary: Algebraic/geometric multigrid as a preconditioner or standalone solver for Ax=b, measured with the setup phase (hierarchy construction: coarsening + interpolation + Galerkin SpGEMM triple product) and the solve phase (V-cycle smoothing + SpMV) reported as fully separate numbers — the split every surveyed solver paper's own code enforces internally, even when its headline speedup blends them. GPU/algebraic-AMG variants and a CPU/ geometric-MG variant are kept separate because they have structurally different hierarchies (SpGEMM-coarsened matrix hierarchy vs. a geometrically-refined structured grid with no comparable "setup phase").
multigrid.operation: solve A[N,N](sparse, s.p.d.) x[N] = b[N] via (P)CG with an AMG/MG V-cycle preconditioner; A_k+1 = R_k A_k P_k for the algebraic-setup variants

variants.claim: steady-state GPU AMG SETUP-phase throughput (coarsening + interpolation + Galerkin triple-product SpGEMM chain that builds the grid hierarchy), reported ENTIRELY separately from solve-phase time — the axis this track's own instructions call out as the classic AMG split, and one that AmgT's and BootCMatchGX's own code/plots both already keep separate internally (AmgT's `t_start/t_stop` bracket around `HYPRE_BoomerAMGSetup` alone; BootCMatchGX's `tsetup` reported apart from `tsolve`). This variant exists so a paper cannot advertise a blended "total speedup" number that hides a setup-time regression behind a solve-time win, or vice versa.

steady-state GPU AMG SOLVE-phase throughput for a FIXED, disconnected- from-convergence iteration count — the protocol AmgT's own driver code actually implements (`HYPRE_BoomerAMGSetMaxIter(precond, 50)` combined with `HYPRE_BoomerAMGSetTol(precond, 1e-20)`, which can never trigger early exit). This variant exists specifically to give every implementation the SAME fixed amount of work (comparable per-iteration throughput, no implementation can "win" by converging in fewer iterations that happen to do less real work) — paired with mg-gpu-e2e-pcg below, which is the honest convergence-gated counterpart this variant alone cannot provide.

end-to-end, CONVERGENCE-GATED preconditioned-CG solve: one-shot AMG setup + PCG iterations to a real stopping tolerance — BootCMatchGX's exact protocol (relative residual < 1e-6 in the l2 norm, capped at 1000 iterations), the honest counterpart to mg-gpu-solve-kernel-fixed-iter's fixed-work number. This is the claim practitioners actually care about ("how long until I have a usable answer"), and the one AmgT's own fixed-iteration/tol=1e-20 protocol structurally cannot answer.

end-to-end CPU multi-core geometric-multigrid throughput (HPCG-style): no separate algebraic setup phase exists for this problem class (the grid hierarchy is defined directly by geometric refinement, factor of 8 per level, not by SpGEMM coarsening from a matrix) — MGopt-APP's exact evaluation shape, kept as its own variant rather than forced into the GPU setup/solve split above, since that split does not apply to a geometrically-generated hierarchy.

nbody.summary: Fixed-radius pairwise-proximity/collision detection for dense spherical-particle systems on GPU ray-tracing hardware (BVH build + RT-core broad/narrow-phase query + integration), measured as interactions/s jointly with an exactness gate, since this track's sole available paper has no tunable accuracy/approximation knob and no energy-conservation notion the way a classical Barnes-Hut/FMM tree-code would (see survey.md Divergences #1-2 for why those two axes from the parent task template do not apply here and are recorded as N/A rather than fabricated).
nbody.operation: collisions[t] = DCD(particles[N] (position, velocity, radius_i), domain (unit cube), substep dt); per substep: rebuild RT bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH) over current particle positions, launch an RT ray-generation kernel that queries the BVH for candidate sphere-sphere pairs (broad phase) and resolves true intersections (narrow phase) in one hardware pass, then integrate position/velocity from resolved collision responses. Exact/exhaustive within the query radius -- not an approximation controlled by a tunable order/resolution parameter.

variants.claim: steady-state per-substep throughput of RT-hardware-accelerated fixed-radius collision detection across a particle-count sweep, with BVH-build / detect / integrate reported as three separate phases (matching the paper's own decomposition) rather than blended into one number

ntt.summary: Number-Theoretic Transform (forward NTT / inverse INTT) over Z_q[x]/(x^N+1) as used inside RNS-CKKS fully homomorphic encryption — this track's single paper (Cheddar) never times bare NTT/INTT in isolation, only as a component slice inside fused elementary-CKKS-op kernels (HMult/HRot/HAdd/Rescale) or whole-FHE-workload runs (bts/HELR/ ResNet/Sort). This spec defines both the isolated microkernel the instructions require (degree, modulus bit-width, batch, correctness vs a reference NTT) and an embedded variant that matches what the paper actually reports, so the two are never conflated.
ntt.operation: Forward: A_hat[i] = sum_{j=0}^{N-1} A[j] * omega^{ij} mod q, for each RNS limb q_i independently (q_i prime, q_i = 1 mod 2N so a primitive 2N-th root of unity omega exists mod q_i); Inverse (INTT) is the scaled conjugate transform, INTT(NTT(A)) = A mod q_i exactly. N is a power of two (this track's paper uses only N=2^16). A polynomial is represented in RNS as L limbs, each an independent length-N vector mod its own q_i; "batch" = number of limbs L processed together (Cheddar fuses all L limbs' NTTs into one kernel launch) and, orthogonally, number of independent ciphertexts/polynomials submitted together (not swept by this track's paper — see survey.md Divergence 3).

variants.claim: Steady-state throughput of a STANDALONE forward+inverse NTT pair (INTT(NTT(x)) round trip, or NTT-only if reporting one direction), decoupled from BConv/automorphism/elementwise ops it is normally fused with in this track's own artifact. This variant does not exist as a ready-to-run benchmark in Cheddar's repo as read; it requires either disabling kernel fusion in Cheddar or invoking a library's raw per-limb NTT device function directly. Included because the instructions require this axis and because Cheddar's own Fig. 3b shows the NTT component is a substantial, separately-optimized (EOT: 1.16x) fraction of a fused kernel's time — isolating it is a reasonable ask, not an invented one.

Steady-state throughput of an elementary CKKS ciphertext op (HMult, HRot, HAdd, or Rescale) that internally issues one or more NTT/INTT calls as part of a fused INTT->BConv->NTT sequence — this is what Cheddar's own Table 7 actually measures, reproduced here as the track's real "kernel-only" number, with the NTT/BConv/other-component time breakdown reported alongside (not hidden) per Cheddar's own Fig. 3b practice.

pagerank.summary: Global PageRank via power iteration over a directed graph in CSR/CSC form, measured both as steady-state per-iteration throughput at a fixed iteration budget and as time-to-convergence under an explicit epsilon, with preprocessing (format conversion, any reordering) strictly separated from iteration time and correctness gated against an independent fp64 reference rank vector.
pagerank.operation: r_{t+1}[v] = (1-alpha)/N + alpha * sum_{u: (u,v) in E} r_t[u] / outdeg(u), for all v in V, iterated from r_0[v] = 1/N until either a fixed iteration budget k is exhausted or ||r_t - r_{t-1}||_1 < epsilon; A[V,V] is the (unweighted, direction-preserving) sparse adjacency, dangling nodes (outdeg(u)=0) redistribute their mass uniformly over all V; damping alpha = 0.85, personalization vector uniform (global PageRank, not personalized/single-source).

variants.claim: steady-state per-iteration kernel throughput at a fixed iteration budget k=20, preprocessing excluded but reported separately — reconciles the track's two competing fixed-count conventions (Corder/Shun20's 1-iteration microbenchmark and GeraK23's 50-iteration cap) at a middle value the track itself already uses for profiling (Corder's own 20-iteration L2-cache-miss figure)

steady-state kernel time-to-convergence under an explicit epsilon, preprocessing excluded — a spec-level FIX to a real gap in the surveyed literature: none of the 4 papers in this track runs PageRank to a disclosed convergence tolerance (see survey.md Divergences #1); this variant exists so the track has at least one apples-to-apples "how long until I actually have a usable rank vector" number, not just fixed/arbitrary iteration-count snapshots

end-to-end throughput including one-shot graph preprocessing (CSR/CSC construction and, if used, a reordering pass), amortized over k=20 iterations — operationalizes ChenC22/Corder's own amortization discipline ("N iterations of PR needed to amortize reordering cost") as a first-class reportable variant instead of a paper footnote, and gives reordering-focused submissions (Corder-style) a variant that measures what they actually contribute, matching the sibling `bfs` benchspec's bfs-e2e-preprocessing / bfs-reordering-cost design for the same reason

particle-in-cell.summary: Explicit electromagnetic particle-in-cell (PIC) cycle (push -> deposit -> field-solve -> interpolate) on a 3D structured grid, benchmarked as particles-processed/s with a per-timestep phase split (interpolation+push / deposition / redistribution) matching this track's sole paper's own decomposition, gated by a per-step charge/energy/ momentum conservation check (see survey.md for why this track's one paper's own diagnostic already matches the parent task's suggested correctness axis almost exactly). This track's paper's own artifact repo is inaccessible (survey.md scope note); the spec is grounded in arXiv fulltext only, flagged throughout wherever repo-level confirmation (exact timer, warmup length) was not obtainable.
particle-in-cell.operation: for each of NT timesteps: (1) Field Interpolation -- interpolate E/B fields from the Yee-staggered grid to each particle's position, reformulated as an MPU-friendly outer-product (3rd-order B-spline shape factors); (2) Push -- advance particle velocity/position via the Boris pusher; (3) Deposition -- scatter each particle's current contribution back to the Yee grid (direct-current deposition); (4) Field solve -- update E/B on the grid (Yee FDTD update, grid-only, not part of the particle-phase timing bucket); (5) Redistribute -- migrate particles that crossed cell/rank boundaries to their new owning rank/cell, asynchronously overlapped with (3).

variants.claim: steady-state particle-phase throughput (particles processed/s) across a particles-per-cell (PPC) sweep, with the paper's own 3-way phase split (interpolation+push / deposit / redistribute) reported separately rather than blended into one number; field-solve (grid-only Yee update) excluded from this variant since it carries no per-particle cost and is not part of what this track's paper contributes on

weak-scaling efficiency of the particle-phase under a particle-migration-heavy stress workload, isolating this paper's central systems contribution (overlapping asynchronous particle redistribution with Deposition) rather than single-node kernel throughput alone -- included as a second variant specifically because variant 1 alone would miss the paper's main claim, which is a multi-node communication-overlap result, not a single-device kernel speedup

preconditioner.summary: Measures preconditioner cost along three axes that the track's own papers keep separate but a benchmark must report together where an outer solver exists: one-shot setup (factorization / hierarchy construction / DAG scheduling), per-application or per-iteration apply cost, and, for variants that exercise an outer Krylov solver, the number of iterations the preconditioner buys or costs versus a reference.
preconditioner.operation: Setup: build M (an approximate inverse of A, or a multigrid hierarchy, or a scheduled DAG) once from sparse A. Apply: z = M*r, either as a standalone kernel proxy (matrix-power A^d*x for polynomial preconditioners; forward/ backward triangular solve for ILU(0)/IC(0)) or nested inside a Krylov solve (PCG/BiCGStab) that is run to a residual-based convergence criterion.

variants.claim: steady-state per-application throughput of the matrix-power kernel A^d*x that underlies polynomial preconditioners, one-shot block- partitioning setup excluded and reported separately; no outer solver exercised (this is a kernel-only proxy, not a solve-to-convergence).

steady-state kernel throughput of ILU(0)/IC(0) triangular-solve apply and sparse-triangular-solve (SpTRSV), with one-shot DAG-scheduling plus factorization setup reported separately; no outer solver exercised.

end-to-end preconditioned-CG time-to-solution on a single GPU, with one-shot preconditioner-setup time, mean per-iteration time, and iteration-count-to-convergence all reported together: a cheap preconditioner that needs 3x the iterations is not faster here.

end-to-end AMG-preconditioned Krylov time-to-solution across multiple GPUs/nodes (strong and weak scaling), with AMG hierarchy setup time, per-iteration time, and iteration-count-to-convergence all reported together, plus operator complexity as a hierarchy-quality indicator.

qr.summary: QR factorization spanning four claims this track's own literature treats as genuinely different: dense single-node/GPU Householder QR with pivoting strategy (none / column-pivoted-RRQR / PAQR's pivoting-avoiding variant) as a required, disclosed parameter alongside shape and rank-deficiency location; distributed ScaLAPACK PDGEQRF at scale with tile size and process grid as required parameters (inheriting ScaLAPACK's own internal residual-check convention); sparse multifrontal QR with symbolic-analysis reordering strategy as a required, disclosed parameter; and batched transform-domain (tensor, "t-QR") QR of many small-to-medium frontal slices. No paper in this 4-paper track targets TSQR/Communication- Avoiding-QR specifically or an explicitly tall-skinny (M >> N) benchmark shape — this is a genuine gap in the track's own literature, not a disagreement to reconcile (see survey.md); this spec's dense variant still sweeps shape (square and tall-skinny) using the Householder/RRQR/PAQR algorithms this track's own papers DO implement, and flags TSQR/CAQR's absence explicitly rather than fabricating evidence for an algorithm none of the surveyed papers run.
qr.operation: A[M,N] = Q[M,M] * R[M,N] (or the economy form Q[M,N]*R[N,N] for M>=N), Q orthogonal (Q^T*Q = I), R upper triangular. Column-pivoted variants additionally produce a permutation Pi such that A*Pi = Q*R with |R_ii| non-increasing (rank-revealing); PAQR produces the same asymptotic cost as unpivoted QR while approaching QRCP's forward-error accuracy on rank-deficient A, WITHOUT physically pivoting columns. Sparse multifrontal QR additionally performs a symbolic fill-reducing reordering pass before numerical factorization. Batched/tensor QR (t-QR) treats a 3rd-order tensor's tube dimension as a batch axis: an M x N x K tensor's t-QR is K independent 2D QR factorizations of the frontal slices in transform (FFT) domain.

variants.claim: steady-state single-node (CPU or single-GPU) dense Householder QR factorization time, with PIVOTING STRATEGY (none / column-pivoted-RRQR / PAQR) and matrix SHAPE (square vs. tall-skinny) both required, disclosed, swept parameters, plus RANK-DEFICIENCY LOCATION as a third swept axis for the rank-deficient cases — this is the axis SidLakhdarCBALGTJWDDA23 (PAQR, this track's central paper) is built around: unpivoted QR (dgeqrf), column-pivoted QRCP (dgeqp3), and PAQR (dgepoqrf) are compared on the SAME matrix at the SAME shape, with deficient-column location (beginning/middle/end/random) itself swept as a first-class parameter, since a pivoting-avoidance algorithm's behavior is sensitive to where in the elimination order the deficiency falls.

distributed (multi-node) dense ScaLAPACK PDGEQRF at scale, with tile size (mb, nb) AND process grid (p, q) as required, disclosed, tunable parameters — matches ChoDKLLL23 (GPTuneCrowd)'s own tuning search space for this exact routine, and inherits ScaLAPACK's own internal factorization-residual gate (FRESID/PASSED against a disclosed THRESH) rather than requiring a separately-implemented correctness check, since this is the one variant in this track where a real correctness gate was found already wired into the literature's own measurement path.

sparse multifrontal QR factorization of a SuiteSparse-collection matrix, with SYMBOLIC-ANALYSIS REORDERING STRATEGY (AMD / COLAMD / METIS / NESDIS, or a learned/adaptive choice among them) as a required, disclosed parameter, reported separately from numerical factorization time — matches LinYWT021 (STM-multifrontal QR)'s own two-part evaluation structure exactly (symbolic analysis and numerical factorization ARE separately timed in its own artifact, per its QR_time.txt's "analysis factorization time, numerical factorization time" columns).

batched QR factorization of many small-to-medium 2D frontal slices from a 3rd-order tensor's transform (FFT) domain representation, with the BATCHING STRATEGY (based / batched / streamed) as a required, disclosed parameter — matches ZhangLWW20 (cuTensor-tubal)'s own t-QR primitive exactly, a genuinely different QR-shape claim from the other three variants (many independent small QRs, not one large matrix).

quantized-gemm.summary: Fused (or explicit) dequantize-then-multiply GEMM for LLM linear layers: a full/half-precision activation matrix times a low-precision weight matrix (INT4/W3/FP6/FP8/INT8, optionally per-group or MX-block scaled), measured across the batch-size axis from memory-bound decode to compute-bound batched/prefill regimes, with model-level accuracy (perplexity delta) reported as a mandatory companion to every speed number, never as an afterthought.
quantized-gemm.operation: C[M,N] = A[M,K](fp16/bf16 activation, row-major) * B[K,N](quantized weight). B is stored packed at b in {3,4,6,8} bits per element (uniform or MX-microscaled), with per-group (default group=128 columns of K) or per-block scale factors s[K/group, N]. Dequantization of B to fp16/bf16 happens either FUSED inside the GEMM kernel (the dominant pattern: MARLIN, Tilus, FP6-LLM, QFactory, Quantix, ZipServ) or as a SEPARATE pre-pass producing a dense fp16 B' consumed by a standard dense GEMM (the naive/explicit baseline every fused kernel is compared against). variant qgemm-w8a8-mx additionally quantizes A (both operands in FP8 E4M3, MX block-scaled).

variants.claim: steady-state fused-dequant kernel throughput in the memory-bound small-batch decode regime (batch=1..32), preprocessing (weight packing/quantization) excluded and reported separately once.

same fused-dequant kernel family and shape suite as qgemm-w4a16-decode-kernel, but swept into the compute-bound large-batch/prefill regime where quantization speedup shrinks or reverses -- FP6-LLM's own numbers show 0.94x (a SLOWDOWN) vs. TensorRT coarse-grained W4A16 at batch=32, invisible if only small batches are reported. This variant exists specifically to prevent single-batch cherry-picking (see survey Divergences).
both-operand-quantized GEMM (INT8 or FP8-E4M3 MX-microscaled), structurally distinct arithmetic from weight-only W4A16 above -- covers MixQ's W8A8 and MXBLAS's MX-FP8 regimes.

mandatory companion measurement, NOT a speed variant: does the quantization scheme (any of the formats above) still produce a usable model? Required to accompany every reported speedup number above -- only 2 of 13 surveyed papers (FP6-LLM, MixQ) treat this as first-class, and the task's own instructions require accuracy alongside speed.

scan-reduction.summary: Associative(-commutative) reduction of n input values, measured three ways this track's literature actually benchmarks: a flat reduction to one scalar (steady-state, memory-bound GB/s vs. achievable HBM bandwidth); a segmented/keyed reduction into H << n output bins (generalized histogram, H swept independently of n); and a cascaded/fused reduction whose running accumulator feeds a downstream consumer op inside one kernel launch (online-softmax-then-GEMM). No surveyed paper implements a literal Blelloch/Hillis-Steele all-prefixes scan; this gap is disclosed rather than papered over (see open_questions).
scan-reduction.operation: flat: out = reduce(op, A[n]) -> scalar. segmented: out[H] = reduce_by_key(op, A[n], key[n] in [0,H)) -> H scalars. fused: running_max[n]/running_sum[n] via an online recurrence over A[n], consumed by a downstream GEMM within the same kernel launch (no intermediate HBM round-trip for the reduction's own output).

variants.claim: steady-state throughput of a flat sum-reduction over a single GPU-resident array to one scalar output, single isolated call — Navarro's own benchmark shape, the only variant with a well-defined memory-traffic lower bound (read n elements once, write 1).

segmented/keyed reduction into H output bins from a single input pass, H swept independently of the fixed input size — Henriksen's own benchmark shape (generalized histograms), and this track's only representation of the "segmented variants" axis. Genuinely a different kernel from scan-reduction-flat-kernel (contention profile and race-resolution strategy both depend on H, not on n alone).

a running/online reduction (running-max, running-sum recurrence across sequential input tiles — the structurally scan-like part of this operation) fused with a downstream consumer op (GEMM) inside one kernel launch, so the reduction's own intermediate output never round-trips through HBM — RedFuser's own benchmark shape (safe softmax -> GEMM, the attention/MoE-routing pattern). Measured as end-to-end latency/speedup vs. an unfused baseline, not raw reduction GB/s, since the claim is specifically about eliminating a round-trip, not about one kernel's isolated bandwidth.

sddmm.summary: Measure Sampled Dense-Dense Matrix Multiplication throughput — computing dot products between rows of two dense matrices only at the nonzero positions of a given sparsity pattern — across the three input traditions (general SuiteSparse, sparse-DNN/DLMC, real GNN graphs) and two precision regimes (fp32/fp16 unstructured Tensor-Core, sub-fp32 quantized) the track's papers actually use, plus an end-to-end fused-attention variant for papers that only report SDDMM embedded in a bigger pipeline.
sddmm.operation: P[i,j] = S[i,j] * dot(A[i,:], B[j,:])  for (i,j) in nnz(S); A: M x K dense, B: N x K dense (row-major), S/P: M x N sparse with identical sparsity pattern

variants.claim: steady-state SDDMM kernel throughput on general (non-DNN) sparse matrices given in CSR, fp32, preprocessing excluded from the timed loop. This is the common denominator most GPU papers in the track report (RoDe, and implicitly the Sputnik/Gale-2020 kernels every later paper baselines against).

steady-state SDDMM kernel throughput using Tensor-Core blocked sparse formats (unstructured sparsity packed into fixed row-window tiles) on real graph-adjacency matrices, fp16/tf32, one-shot block preprocessing excluded from steady-state but reported separately. Matches FlashSparse's and Fused3S's own kernel-only tables.

quantized (sub-fp32) SDDMM kernel throughput on sparsity-controlled sparse-DNN weight matrices, isolating numeric precision as the axis of comparison — Magicube's contribution is a genuinely distinct numerical regime from the fp32/fp16 variants above and cannot be fairly folded into either.

end-to-end fused SDDMM + softmax + SpMM ("3S" sparse-attention) pipeline cost, one-shot preprocessing (block partition / row-window layout) amortized over k=100 repeated forward passes — the context most track papers actually deploy SDDMM in (GNN attention / graph embedding), and the only number several papers (Fused3S headline figures, FusedMM's end-to-end Force2Vec runs, FlashSparse's GCN/AGNN tables) report at all. Isolated SDDMM-stage cost is additionally reported via kernel-name profiling so this variant stays comparable to sddmm-tensorcore-blocked-fp16.

sequence-alignment.summary: Pairwise dynamic-programming sequence alignment (Smith-Waterman local / Needleman-Wunsch global-semi-global, exact or X-drop-approximate), plus the two end-to-end genome-mapping pipelines (BWA-MEM-class short-read mapping, LASTZ-class whole-genome alignment) that use a pairwise-alignment kernel as one stage of a larger seed/index -> filter -> extend pipeline. The surveyed literature splits along two axes that cannot be collapsed into one variant: exact-optimal vs. deliberately-approximate (X-drop) scoring, and kernel-only DP throughput vs. end-to-end pipeline throughput with a one-shot index/table build.
sequence-alignment.operation: H[i,j] = max( H[i-1,j-1] + sigma(q_i, s_j), E[i,j], F[i,j], nu )  — the standard SW/NW recurrence over query Q (length n) and subject S (length m), sigma a substitution function (simple match/mismatch or a matrix such as BLOSUM62), E/F the linear- or affine-gap auxiliary matrices; variants 3-4 wrap this kernel inside seed -> filter/index -> extend pipelines.

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput for EXACT optimal pairwise alignment (Smith-Waterman local / Needleman-Wunsch global / semi-global), preprocessing excluded. The common denominator of AnySeq, MASA-CUDAlign/MultiBP, and the futhark-mem-sc22 `nw` benchmark — all three compute a provably optimal score (MultiBP's block pruning is lossless by construction, not an approximation).

steady-state kernel throughput for X-drop / banded APPROXIMATE local alignment, preprocessing excluded. LOGAN's own scenario — deliberately NOT held to the exact-DP correctness bar above, since X-drop is a pruned heuristic by design.

end-to-end short-read mapping pipeline throughput (one-shot index build + align a full real read set), correctness gated by BIT-EXACT output match to a named reference tool. FastAlign's own stated bar ("100% identical output to BWA-MEM").

end-to-end whole-genome pairwise alignment (seed -> GPU filter -> extend) throughput including one-shot per-target-genome index/seed- table construction, correctness gated by "recovers every alignment the named baseline tool finds" (a superset gate, not equality). SegAlign's own stated bar.

set-intersection.summary: Per-edge sorted-adjacency-list set intersection (Jaccard-weight computation: |N(u) intersect N(v)| / |N(u) union N(v)| for every edge (u,v) in a graph), swept across list-length/degree skew and intersection selectivity, comparing a degree-aware binned kernel (tuned search-group-size/assembly-size per degree bin) against fixed-configuration GPU baselines and a CPU multi-core algorithm, all from the same codebase for an apples-to-apples comparison.
set-intersection.operation: Given graph G=(V,E) in CSR (sorted neighbor lists per vertex): for every edge (u,v) in E, compute J(u,v) = |N(u) intersect N(v)| / |N(u) union N(v)|, where N(u), N(v) are u's and v's sorted neighbor-id arrays (list-merge-style intersection, O(deg(u)+deg(v)) per edge naively). Output: one Jaccard weight per edge, in CSR edge order.

variants.claim: steady-state GPU kernel throughput for the degree-aware binned intersection kernel (edges bucketed by endpoint degree, each bin run with a search-group-size g / assembly-size a configuration), compared against fixed-(g,a) GPU baselines from the SAME repo (naive one-thread(-team)-per-edge, cuGraph) -- binning/ML-model- inference (choosing g,a per bin) counted as one-shot preprocessing, reported separately.

steady-state CPU shared-memory multi-core throughput for the SAME Jaccard-weight computation, using the paper's own proposed traditional-but-effective CPU algorithm -- claimed by the paper to perform "comparably" to the GPU algorithms; this variant makes that claim independently checkable rather than asserted.

signed-graph-balancing.summary: Parallel discovery and balancing of all fundamental cycles in a large signed graph (edges labeled +/-) via linear-time vertex/edge labeling, measured as fundamental-cycles-balanced-per-second, with the number of edges flipped reported as a solution-quality metric since the algorithm is a linear-time heuristic, not a proven-minimum edge-flip solver.
signed-graph-balancing.operation: (labels[V], flipped_edges[E']) = graphB_plus(G=(V,E,sign: E -> {+,-}), iterations); builds a spanning tree, computes vertex/edge labels via path-compressed union-find, enumerates all |E|-|V|+1 fundamental cycles from non-tree edges, and flips the minimum-weight edge per imbalanced cycle so the whole graph becomes sign-balanced (every cycle has an even count of negative edges).

variants.claim: steady-state balancing-phase throughput (spanning tree + labeling + cycle detection/traversal/flip) on the union of real signed-graph datasets used by this track's paper; CSV parsing/graph read excluded but reported separately (one-shot, not amortized)

same-algorithm GPU-vs-CPU comparison across graph scale, isolating the parallelization contribution from the algorithmic contribution (both implementations exist in the paper's own repo) — needed because a bare "our GPU is fast" number is only meaningful against the paper's own CPU baseline of the SAME method, not a black-box "prior work" comparison

sparse-attention-kernel.summary: Fused attention restricted to a 0/1 sparsity mask (softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d) + mask)V computed only over allowed positions), measured as steady-state kernel throughput with BOTH an effective (mask-nnz-based) and a dense-equivalent FLOP count reported side by side so speedup claims state which convention they use, split into a structured/swept-ratio variant (sequence-based, sparsity ratio as a first-class swept parameter) and a real-graph-adjacency variant (Fused3S's GNN-style sparse attention, where sparsity is a fixed dataset property, not a tunable knob) — plus a mandatory downstream quality-gate report that no surveyed paper currently provides.
sparse-attention-kernel.operation: O[B,H,S,d] = softmax( (Q[B,H,S,d] @ K[B,H,S,d]^T) / sqrt(d) + mask ) @ V[B,H,S,d], mask in {0,-inf}^{S x S} (or, for the graph-adjacency variant, O[N,d] = softmax_row(A ⊙ (Q K^T / sqrt(d))) V over N = graph node count and A = the graph's sparse adjacency matrix in CSR)

variants.claim: steady-state fused sparse-attention kernel throughput under a structured, parametrically-swept sparsity mask (sliding-window, block-local+global, dilated, or a model-defined dynamic/regional ViT mask), at a stated and measured sparsity ratio, with preprocessing (mask/adjacency construction, structural reordering, ILP-schedule solve, autotuning/operator-fusion search) excluded from per-iteration time and reported separately. This is the common denominator STOF's `benchmk_attn_unified.py` and TomczakK25's 6 kernel variants both measure, and what ipdps-26_vit's ILP-scheduled tile execution is a drop-in candidate for (its DynamicViT/RegionViT/VisionLongformer masks are treated as fixed sparsity patterns at their own native ratio, submitted at whatever Sf they produce).

steady-state fused SDDMM+softmax+SpMM graph-attention kernel throughput over a REAL graph's own sparse adjacency (not a synthetic or parametrically-swept mask), preprocessing (CSR to tensor-core-block conversion) excluded and reported separately. This is Fused3S's own claim and the only legitimate comparison point for it — its "sparsity ratio" is a fixed dataset property (typically <1% density for citation/social graphs), not a value any candidate chooses, so pooling it with the structured-mask variant above would force an artificial ratio framing onto data that does not have one.

sparse-factorization.summary: Sparse direct factorization of a matrix stored in a sparse format — nonsymmetric LU (partial pivoting or threshold pivoting), SPD Cholesky, or (possibly rectangular) QR — via a fill-reducing-ordering + symbolic-analysis + numeric-factorization pipeline, measured so that ordering cost, symbolic cost, and numeric cost are never silently merged into one number unless the variant says so explicitly.
sparse-factorization.operation: LU family: P*A*Q = L*U  (A[N,N] sparse nonsymmetric, P/Q permutations from pivoting/ordering, L unit-lower-triangular, U upper-triangular, both sparse with fill-in beyond A's nonzero pattern). Cholesky family: P*A*P^T = L*L^T (A[N,N] sparse SPD, P a fill-reducing symmetric permutation, L sparse lower-triangular). QR family: A*Q_col = Q*R (A[M,N] sparse, M>=N typical; Q_col a column-fill-reducing permutation, Q orthogonal (implicit, Householder/ multifrontal), R sparse upper-triangular).

variants.claim: steady-state SYMBOLIC factorization time only (fill-in pattern / elimination-tree or supernode-partition computation), with the fill-reducing ordering computed once beforehand and given as a fixed, pre-permuted input matrix — NOT counted in this variant's timed region. This mirrors gSoFa's own methodology exactly (its README states the reordered matrix is dumped once from SuperLU_DIST and fed to gSoFa "for fair comparison"), generalized here to all three factorization families so LU/Cholesky/QR symbolic phases are comparable on the same protocol. This is the track's common-denominator variant: it is the only phase gSoFa's paper reports at all, and it isolates the graph/combinatorial cost from the floating-point cost.

steady-state NUMERIC factorization time/throughput given a precomputed ordering AND precomputed symbolic structure (nonzero counts/positions of L/U, L, or R already known) — matches swCholesky's scoping (ordering given via precomputed permutation files) and PanguLU's per-phase GFLOP/s reporting of its numeric-factorization stage specifically. Tile/block size (PanguLU's `-nb`, or the analogous supernode-merge parameter in Cholesky/QR) MUST be disclosed per run as a required CLI argument, not a silent default — this is PanguLU's own interface convention (`pangulu_example.elf -nb <block_size> -f <matrix>`) and matches this benchmark suite's sibling `cholesky` track's fairness rule.

how much the CHOICE of fill-reducing ordering algorithm affects downstream numeric-factorization time, fill-in ratio, and memory, on a fixed matrix suite — makes explicit what STM-multifrontal-QR's paper studies directly (its entire contribution is picking AMD vs. COLAMD vs. METIS vs. NESDIS per-matrix via a learned classifier) and what GPTuneCrowd instead folds invisibly into one bundled runtime number by treating ordering (`COLPERM`) as just another autotuned knob. This variant is this spec's answer to "fill-reducing ordering in or out of scope": it is IN scope, but as an independent, disclosed, swept axis — never silently fixed to one method and never silently hidden inside an end-to-end number.

end-to-end wall time — ordering + symbolic analysis + numeric factorization + one triangular solve — amortized over k repeated numeric factorizations of the SAME sparsity pattern with fresh values (or a fresh RHS), reflecting the realistic HPC usage pattern GPTuneCrowd's own NIMROD case study exercises: a fixed mesh/matrix nonzero pattern, ordering computed once, but each of NIMROD's 30 time-marching steps triggers a fresh block-Jacobi numeric factorization via SuperLU_DIST. k=30 is chosen to match that real-usage number exactly (GPTuneCrowd: "we set the number of time steps to 30"); k MUST be disclosed and preprocessing cost MUST be reported both as a one-shot absolute number and as its per-iteration amortized contribution (preproc_time / k), never silently merged into a per-iteration average without that breakdown.

sparse-format-conversion.summary: Converting a sparse matrix from a source storage format (CSR/COO as loaded) to a target format optimized for a downstream sparse kernel (here: SpMM), covering both the pure conversion throughput and the end-to-end, format-selection-amortized usage pattern this track's one surveyed paper (LiteForm) actually implements.
sparse-format-conversion.operation: target_format = convert(source_format, A[M,K]); optionally target_format_selection = select(A) when the target format itself is chosen automatically per-matrix (LiteForm's CELL-vs-BCSR classifier + CELL partition-count regressor + bucket-config search).

variants.claim: steady-state, format-pair-specific conversion throughput (nnz/s), source format given/loaded, target format's construction timed in isolation from any downstream SpMM call — the "just the conversion" number this track's axis list asks for, which LiteForm's own artifact does not report as a standalone metric (it only reports conversion-stage wall time as part of a 3-stage preprocessing breakdown ahead of an SpMM run, never isolated on its own).

end-to-end throughput: one-shot format selection + conversion + partition/bucket-config search, amortized over k repeated SpMM calls on the same matrix — this is what LiteForm's own released driver (drive05.spmm.end-to-end.sh -> proc05.spmm.end-to-end.py) actually measures, so k and the pipeline stages are reproduced from it rather than invented.

sparse-tensor-contraction.summary: Contraction of sparse tensors/matrices under an einsum-style index-contraction specification, covering three structurally distinct sub-problems found in this track's literature: sparse(A)-times-dense(B) GPU kernels expressed as indirect einsums over fixed-length sparse formats (Insum), true sparse-tensor x sparse- tensor contraction (SpGETT) over FROSTT N-mode tensors (parTC), and fused multi-kernel composite sparse-tensor-algebra expression chains built by loop-nest restructuring (SparseLNR). No single input suite or reference kernel spans all three, so this spec defines one variant per sub-problem rather than forcing an artificial common denominator, following the same resolution used by the sibling tensor-contraction track for its four shape families.
sparse-tensor-contraction.operation: General form: given sparse tensor(s)/matrice(s) {A, B, ...} and an einsum-style index-contraction expression, compute the output tensor C by contracting the specified shared indices, where at least one operand is sparse (stored in a compressed format that skips explicit zeros) and the output may itself be dense (sparse-times-dense case) or sparse (sparse-times-sparse case, with a data-dependent, not-known-a-priori output nonzero count). Format conversion and/or any index-permutation required to align operand layouts is scoped explicitly per variant below (never silently amortized into per-call time unless stated).

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput of GPU sparse(-structured or -unstructured) times dense einsum kernels expressed via fixed-length sparse formats (GroupCOO/BlockGroupCOO) and executed as fully-fused gather-matmul-scatter Triton/Tensor-Core kernels, format conversion and compile/autotune time reported separately

steady-state kernel throughput of general sparse-tensor x sparse-tensor contraction (SpGETT) on real N-mode sparse tensors from FROSTT, preprocessing (hash-table/index construction) excluded and reported separately once

steady-state throughput of fused, multi-operator composite sparse-tensor- algebra expressions (e.g. SDDMM->SpMM->GEMM chains) generated via loop-nest restructuring, compared against separately-scheduled and single-perfectly-nested-loop TACO baselines, codegen/compile time reported separately

spatial-join.summary: GPU spatial join: line segment intersection (LSI) and point-in-polygon (PIP) testing between two real geospatial polygon/polyline datasets, measured with index (BVH/grid) BUILD time reported separately from QUERY time, across a uniform-grid baseline, a software-BVH baseline, and an RT-hardware-accelerated implementation all sharing one codebase, plus an external GPU-library baseline, with full double-precision-equivalent correctness required despite RT hardware's native precision limits.
spatial-join.operation: LSI: given two sets of polyline chains R (base map) and S (query map), find every pair of segments (r in R, s in S) that geometrically intersect, and the intersection point. PIP: given a point set P and a polygon set (represented as R's chains), determine for each point p in P which polygon (if any) of R contains it. Polygon overlay: combine LSI+PIP results to compute the full overlay of R and S (every resulting face and which R-polygon/S-polygon pair it came from).

variants.claim: steady-state LSI and PIP query throughput across three index strategies sharing one codebase (uniform grid, software LBVH, RT-hardware-accelerated BVH), with index BUILD cost reported separately from query time -- since BVH build is explicitly the paper's own second stated bottleneck alongside precision recovery, collapsing build+query into one number would hide exactly the tradeoff the paper's contribution targets.

spectral-sparsification.summary: Incremental spectral sparsification of a large undirected weighted graph: nearly-linear-time initial sparsifier construction followed by O(log N)-time per-edge-batch incremental updates, measured as time jointly with the relative condition number between original and sparsifier Laplacians, since sparsification quality and edge-count reduction are an inherent tradeoff with no single correct answer.
spectral-sparsification.operation: H_0 = Setup(G_0=(V,E_0,w): Laplacian L_{G_0}) via low-resistance- diameter (LRD) decomposition into node clusters, selecting a spectrally -critical edge subset; H_i = Update(H_{i-1}, Delta E_i (new weighted edges)) in O(log N) time per update using low-dimensional resistance embeddings to score edge importance/redundancy; output H_i is a sparse weighted graph (subgraph, not necessarily edge-subset of G) whose Laplacian spectrally approximates L_{G_i}.

variants.claim: steady-state one-shot setup-phase time (initial sparsifier construction from scratch) on the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection suite used by this track's paper; this is the common denominator any spectral sparsifier must support before incremental updates are possible

per-update O(log N) incremental throughput across a sequence of 10 edge-batch insertions per graph, amortized over the batch (this operationalizes the paper's actual headline contribution — up to 200x speedup over full re-sparsification — as a first-class variant rather than folding it into the one-shot setup number)
