spgemm.summary: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication throughput and scaling, covering the single-device steady-state kernel (symbolic+numeric, format-conversion excluded), the amortized end-to-end cost including one-shot format conversion / row reordering, a tensor-core / mixed- precision variant, and distributed multi-GPU strong scaling.
spgemm.operation: C = A[M,K](sparse, CSR) * A[K,M](sparse, CSR)  — self-product (A x A); A x A^T and general A x B as noted secondary modes

variants.claim: steady-state device-side SpGEMM kernel throughput for C = A^2 in fp64, one-time A/B format conversion excluded (reported separately, once); symbolic (size-determination) phase and the result matrix's device memory allocation are INCLUDED, since they are unavoidable, data-dependent per-call costs, not amortizable preprocessing.

end-to-end cost including one-shot format conversion / row reordering, amortized over k=100 repeated SpGEMM calls on the SAME sparsity pattern — answers "is the preprocessing worth it," following clusterwise-spgemm's own break-even-iteration methodology rather than hiding the preprocessing cost in a single figure caption.

tensor-core / mixed-precision SpGEMM throughput (fp16 storage or a variable-precision block format, fp32 accumulation), against the fp64 baseline's correctness and the fp64 baseline's kernel-only time from spgemm-square-kernel-f64 as the speedup reference.

distributed multi-GPU/multi-node strong-scaling throughput and parallel efficiency for C = A^2 on large unstructured matrices that do not fit a single device, holding the matrix fixed and sweeping GPU/node count.

spiking-neural-network.summary: GPGPU simulation of a Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) spiking neural network over a fixed simulated biological duration, measuring wall-time throughput (real-time factor) as a function of network topology (population count/size, local-vs-remote connectivity mix), simulated timestep count, and activity sparsity (firing rate), with a spike-train correctness gate against a reference (non-GPU or higher-precision) simulation required before any speed number counts.
spiking-neural-network.operation: For a network of P populations of N_p LIF neurons each, connected by weighted/delayed synaptic projections (dense within-population, sparse cross-population — the paper's own topology fixes ~80% of projections to front/rear-neighbor populations and ~20% to arbitrary remote populations): simulate T timesteps of dt=0.1ms each, where each timestep updates every neuron's membrane potential V_i(t+dt) = V_i(t)*decay + I_syn_i(t), emits a spike (and resets V_i) when V_i crosses threshold, and propagates that spike's synaptic current to all post-synaptic neurons after the projection's configured delay.

variants.claim: steady-state simulation throughput (simulated-ms of network activity per wall-clock-second, i.e. real-time factor) for a fixed LIF network topology and firing-rate regime, network-construction / IR-compilation excluded and reported separately once. Matches BSim's own test/gpu/standard_test.cpp harness and its GeNN comparison points.

spmm.summary: Sparse matrix times dense matrix (SpMM), the dominant kernel behind GNN message passing, pruned/quantized DNN inference, and iterative sparse solvers; measured as steady-state throughput with preprocessing reported separately, across GPU tensor-core, GPU CUDA-core, CPU, and quantized variants that the surveyed literature treats as genuinely different claims.

variants.claim: steady-state GPU kernel throughput, sparse format given (no runtime conversion), fp32. The common denominator most GPU SpMM papers (RoDe, GE-SpMM, SMaT, DTC-SpMM's inner kernel) actually report.

end-to-end throughput including one-shot sparse-format conversion / reordering (e.g. TCA block reordering for tensor-core layouts, ASpT/ Sputnik/RoDe's row-decomposition preprocessing), amortized over k=100 repeated SpMM calls on the same matrix — the realistic GNN-training usage pattern (EPPGCN benchmarks 100 training epochs; DTC-SpMM's TCA-reordering is a one-time cost paid before an N-sweep of repeated calls).
steady-state CPU kernel throughput, all physical cores, fp32 — the CPU analogue of the GPU kernel variant (FusedMM, SparseLNR, RASSM all target this).

quantized low-precision SpMM throughput on Tensor Cores (int4/int8/ mixed, e.g. Magicube's 4b4b/8b4b/8b8b/16b8b configs) — not commensurable with the fp32 GFLOP/s variants above since the arithmetic is exact integer MAC, but a first-class variant because a meaningful cluster of the track's papers (Magicube, InferFast, NM-SpMM, GeneralSparse) target exactly this.

spmspv.summary: Sparse matrix times sparse vector (SpMSpV), where both the nonzero PATTERN and the resulting output density of the vector operand are first-class variables rather than fixed at "dense." Measured primarily as a function of swept input-vector density on a fixed matrix suite (the axis this track's own papers treat as central), with a second variant driven by a real, workload-generated non-uniform sparsity trace (BFS frontiers) since a synthetic sweep and a real trajectory are not interchangeable, plus a construction-cost variant for the bitmap/index structures several techniques in this track require.
spmspv.operation: y[M](sparse, nnz_y variable) = A[M,K](sparse, CSR/CSC/bitmap) * x[K](sparse, nnz_x swept); output nnz_y is NOT known a priori and must be produced (allocated/compacted) by the kernel, unlike SpMV where the output is always a fully-populated dense M-vector.

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput as a function of INPUT VECTOR DENSITY, swept from near-empty to fully dense on a FIXED matrix — the controlled-sensitivity-curve variant LiAY21 runs directly and the one this track's whole point is to compare across implementations at matched density, not just at one arbitrarily chosen sparsity level.

throughput across the REAL, non-uniform sparsity trajectory a level-synchronous BFS actually produces (frontier density rises then falls across levels, the "small-world bulge" BLEST's own numbers exhibit), as opposed to spmspv-density-sweep-kernel's synthetic uniform ramp — kept as its own variant because a technique tuned to do well on a smooth synthetic sweep is not guaranteed to do well on the bursty, workload-driven density sequence real graph algorithms generate, and this is the actual production use case for SpMSpV in this track (BLEST) and one of two real applications LiAY21 evaluates against.

end-to-end throughput including one-shot structure construction (format conversion, bitmap/BVSS packing, or load-balancing preprocessing), amortized over k=100 calls at a FIXED representative density (10%, chosen as a realistic mid-sparsity operating point neither fully sparse nor fully dense) — the construction-cost analogue of benchspecs/spmv/spec.yaml's spmv-e2e-preproc, needed here because BLEST's BVSS structure and LiAY21's load-balancing preprocessing are both nontrivial one-shot costs neither paper's own artifact clearly amortizes with a stated k.

spmv.summary: Sparse matrix times dense vector (SpMV), the core kernel behind iterative solvers (CG/GMRES/AMG), graph algorithms (GraphBLAS BFS/PageRank), and similarity search; measured as steady-state throughput with format construction reported separately, plus dedicated variants for the conversion-amortized, sequence-of-calls, and symmetric-storage claims that this track's literature treats as genuinely different from a single isolated y=Ax call.

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput, sparse format given/constructed once (construction excluded from the per-call number but measured and reported), single isolated y=Ax call. The common denominator every surveyed paper except FBMPK and AmgT actually reports; run at both fp64 (primary) and fp32 (secondary) since the track splits roughly evenly (fp64: TileSpMV, DCS-SpMV, CB-SpMV; fp32: AlphaSparse, Bit-GraphBLAS, Serpens).

end-to-end throughput including one-shot format construction (mechanical conversion), amortized over k=100 repeated calls on the SAME matrix — the realistic reuse pattern for iterative solvers/AMG/graph algorithms that call SpMV many times per matrix factorization (AmgT: 31 SpMV calls per V-cycle x up to 50 iterations = up to 1,551 calls, so k=100 is conservative relative to real solver usage; DCS-SpMV's own reported numbers already average over 100 calls, just without folding in construction cost).

throughput on a bounded SEQUENCE of SpMV calls on the same matrix A with related vectors (Ax, A^2 x, ..., A^k x, or linear combinations), the Krylov-subspace / multigrid usage pattern that FBMPK targets directly and AmgT exhibits inside its V-cycle — distinct from a single isolated call because cache/reuse effects across the sequence and reordering that only pays off over multiple calls change what "fast" means.

steady-state throughput exploiting matrix symmetry (half-storage, lower- or upper-triangular CSR), for the numerically-symmetric subset of the standard suite — kept as its OWN variant rather than a data filter on spmv-csr-kernel because the computational kernel itself differs: a symmetric SpMV writes to both y[i] and y[j] per stored nonzero (requiring conflict-free or atomic accumulation across threads), a correctness dimension the general kernel never faces, and because GFLOP/s must be counted against the FULL unfolded nnz, not stored nnz, to stay comparable to spmv-csr-kernel at all.

sptrsv.summary: Sparse triangular solve (SpTRSV), L*x=b for x with L sparse lower- triangular, the core kernel behind sparse-direct-solver back-substitution and ILU/IC-preconditioned Krylov iterations; measured with the analysis/scheduling (level-set, DAG-partitioning, codelet-mining, warp-partitioning -- whatever the technique needs to prepare a parallel execution plan) split out as its OWN first-class variant rather than a footnote, because for several of this track's own papers that analysis step IS the contribution, plus a steady-state solve variant, a repeated-solve amortized variant, and a distributed-memory strong-scaling variant for the one surveyed paper (SC'23) whose claim is genuinely different in kind (multi-node/multi-GPU, real LU-factor input) from the other four single-device papers.
sptrsv.operation: solve L[n,n](sparse triangular) * x[n] = b[n](dense) for x

variants.claim: steady-state solve-phase wall time on a single CPU node or single GPU, single RHS (nrhs=1), analysis/scheduling done once beforehand and EXCLUDED from this number (see sptrsv-analysis-phase for that cost as its own first-class measurement, not silently dropped). This is the one denominator all 5 surveyed papers' code actually separates out, even though they disagree on how many times to repeat it and what statistic to report (survey.md Divergence #2).

cost of the one-shot analysis/scheduling step itself, reported as a FIRST-CLASS benchmark result rather than folded silently into "preprocessing, mentioned once" or (worse) re-measured repeatedly inside a solve-timing loop the way Split_SpTRSV's own artifact does. This matters because for 2 of the 5 surveyed papers (HDagg, partially-strided-codelet) the analysis/scheduling ALGORITHM is the paper's actual contribution, not the solve kernel itself -- comparing only solve-phase numbers would erase exactly what those papers are claiming to improve.

end-to-end time = one-shot analysis + k repeated solve calls on the SAME matrix L with DIFFERENT right-hand sides, amortized -- the realistic ILU(0)/IC(0)-preconditioned-Krylov usage pattern (each preconditioned Krylov iteration issues one L-solve and one U-solve; HDagg's own paper targets exactly this via its ILU/IC evaluation) and the factorize-once-solve-many pattern SuperLU_DIST's own pddrive3d1.c driver exists to demonstrate ("we factorize A only once... and reuse... in the subsequent call"). k=50 is chosen as a conservative middle-of-the-road Krylov restart-cycle length (smaller than the SpMV track's k=100, since each SpTRSV "iteration" here already implies 2 kernel calls -- L-solve then U-solve -- for the same nominal iteration count, so 50 keeps total kernel-call count in the same order of magnitude as the SpMV variant's 100 single-matrix calls).

strong-scaling wall time / speedup of a distributed-memory (MPI, multi-node, optionally multi-GPU) SpTRSV across a fixed sequence of process/GPU counts, on a matrix derived from a REAL numeric LU factorization with genuine fill-in -- not the structural-proxy triangular factor used by the other 3 variants. This is a genuinely different claim, not a stricter version of the single-node variants: only 1 of the 5 surveyed papers (SC'23) operates at this scale, and its own baseline comparison is against other distributed algorithms, not cuSPARSE/MKL.

sssp.summary: Single-source shortest paths on a weighted directed or undirected graph (CSR), measured as steady-state kernel time with preprocessing (format conversion, initial delta-parameter selection) strictly separated from per-search kernel time; source-vertex selection and edge-weight distribution are made explicit, disclosed axes rather than silent defaults, since this track's own papers disagree sharply on both.
sssp.operation: dist[V] = SSSP(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, CSR), weight w: E -> R+, source in V); dist[v] = shortest-path weight sum from source to v (INF-sentinel for unreachable v); output additionally includes a parent/predecessor array so correctness can be checked as a valid shortest-path tree, not merely a distance vector.

variants.claim: steady-state search-phase kernel time on named real-world weighted graphs, with the edge-weight distribution and delta-stepping (or equivalent priority-coarsening) parameter selection method both mandatorily disclosed; preprocessing (CSR construction, initial delta computation) excluded but reported separately

end-to-end throughput including one-shot preprocessing (CSR conversion, weight-array construction, and initial delta selection if static), amortized over k=64 searches — same k as the kernel-only variant's repetition count and the bfs spec's e2e variant, so the amortization argument stays apples-to-apples across both tracks

cost of updating a pre-existing, already-correct SSSP tree after a batch of edge insertions/deletions, compared against the cost of recomputing SSSP from scratch on the changed graph — operationalizes the dynamic-SSSP-update literature's own (well-reasoned) rejection of throughput-style metrics as a first-class variant instead of an implicit footnote, directly modeled on the Srinivasan-et-al./Khanda family's evaluation discipline

cost/benefit of the delta-stepping (or equivalent priority- coarsening) parameter choice on its own terms: the delta-vs-time and delta-vs-work-performed curves, and the selection method's own overhead if runtime-dynamic — makes the single sharpest cross-paper divergence in this track (see survey.md notes_on_fairness #5) a first-class, reportable result instead of a hidden hyperparameter buried in a single hand-picked number, directly modeled on ADDS's Figure 7 and GraphIt's per-graph delta table

stencil.summary: Throughput of an iterative structured-grid stencil sweep — a fixed weighted sum over a small neighborhood (star or box support) applied to every point of a dense D-dimensional grid, repeated for T time steps with double-buffered (ping-pong) storage — across three hardware/implementation classes the track's papers actually target: general-purpose CPU/GPU compute (spatial and temporal blocking), Tensor-Core matmul reformulations (fp16), and full domain-application solvers.
stencil.operation: U_out[p] = sum_{d in support(shape, radius r)} w_d * U_in[p + d]  for every interior grid point p, applied for T sequential time steps via double buffering (U_in/U_out swap each step); shape in {star, box}, dims in {1D, 2D, 3D}; star-r has 2*dims*r+1 support points, box-r has (2r+1)^dims support points; halo of width r (periodic or fixed) surrounds the domain.

variants.claim: Steady-state per-time-step throughput of an iterative structured-grid stencil sweep on general-purpose CPU/GPU compute (SIMD/CUDA-core vectorized kernels with spatial and/or temporal blocking), independent of any Tensor-Core matmul reformulation. This is the common denominator across AN5D, PERKS, K-Athena's core update kernel, Devito's generated code, AOStencil, and StencilsOnFPGA.

Throughput of stencil-as-(sparse)-matrix-multiplication reformulations executing on Tensor Cores / Sparse Tensor Cores at fp16, with the one-shot layout/format-construction preprocessing excluded from the timed sweep loop but measured once and reported separately (not merely excluded and left unquantified, as SPIDER's own artifact does).

End-to-end wall-clock speedup of a full domain-application solver (whole program: boundary handling, multi-kernel physics, no I/O) over its own unoptimized/decomposed baseline, for a domain-realistic, CFL- or convergence-order-determined number of steps — reported ALONGSIDE, never substituted for, a kernel-only number from variant 1/2 when both exist for the same code (WindStencil's own README already separates "kernel-focused gain" from "full-application gain"; this variant standardizes that split for the whole track).

string-regex-matching.summary: Multi-pattern regular-expression / finite-automata matching over a byte stream, measured as steady-state matching throughput in Gbps with automaton compilation/preprocessing strictly separated (and, where the literature's own contribution IS compilation, amortized over an explicit k), plus a distinct single-match latency variant for architectures (e.g. FPGA DSAs) that are not naturally described by a corpus-throughput number.
string-regex-matching.operation: matches[] = MATCH(automaton A (NFA | DFA | custom ISA, compiled from a ruleset of R regular expressions), input stream S (bytes)); output is the set of (pattern_id, end_position) pairs where A accepts a prefix of S ending at that position (standard automata-processing semantics — this is NOT single-pattern substring search, it is simultaneous multi-pattern matching, the shape every paper in this track actually benchmarks).

variants.claim: steady-state matching throughput over a fixed input corpus with the automaton supplied ALREADY COMPILED (RE-to-automaton compilation excluded from the timed region but reported once, separately) — the common denominator matching how ngAP, GSpecPal, and 0002PJ20 all actually benchmark (automata ship pre-converted in their artifacts)

end-to-end throughput including one-shot RE-to-automaton compilation (parsing, FSA construction, any merging/optimization), amortized over k matching passes — for tracks where compilation IS the paper's contribution (MFSA's automata-merging, Cicero's MLIR compiler pipeline), following MFSA's own excellent practice of reporting compilation time as a detailed, separately-visible stage breakdown rather than folding it silently into a blended number

per-match latency and energy for a single regular expression against a bounded input, for architectures (FPGA DSAs, or any design not naturally described by a streaming-corpus-throughput number) whose own claimed contribution is latency/energy per operation rather than aggregate bytes/second — follows Cicero's own metric framing rather than forcing an artificial Gbps conversion onto a design that was never built for streaming-corpus throughput

svd.summary: Singular Value Decomposition, in this track's own form: t-SVD, the tensor generalization computed by applying an FFT along a tensor's 3rd (tube) mode and then computing k independent ordinary matrix SVDs of the resulting m x n frequency-domain frontal slices (k = batch/tube depth), followed by an inverse FFT. The track's two papers exercise the FULL (untruncated, one-shot, library-primitive) case and the TRUNCATED (low-tubal-rank, iteratively-called-inside-an-ALS-loop) case respectively — kept as separate variants below (see survey.md's Divergences).
svd.operation: T[m,n,k] = U[m,r,k] * S[r,r,k] * V[n,r,k]^T (per-frontal-slice, in the Fourier domain along the 3rd mode), where r=min(m,n) for the FULL case or r=target-tubal-rank < min(m,n) for the TRUNCATED case; computed as T_hat = fft(T, dim=3); for each of the k frontal slices, [U_hat(:,:,i), S_hat(:,:,i), V_hat(:,:,i)] = svd(T_hat(:,:,i)) (optionally truncated to rank r); U,S,V = ifft(U_hat,S_hat,V_hat, dim=3).

variants.claim: steady-state, one-shot FULL t-SVD (every singular value/vector of every frontal slice, no rank truncation) throughput on synthetic dense tensors, with the based/streamed/batched EXECUTION STRATEGY as a required, disclosed parameter (matching cuTensor-Tubal's own benchmark practice of sweeping all three), and BOTH square and tall-skinny frontal-slice shapes swept (the square-only practice both papers in this track actually use is called out explicitly as insufficient for this track's own "matrix shapes" key axis -- see notes_on_fairness).

end-to-end low-tubal-rank tensor completion via alternating minimization, where a TRUNCATED t-SVD (target tubal-rank r, a required, disclosed, swept parameter -- this track's accuracy/compression tolerance axis) is called once per iteration, amortized over the iterations needed to converge -- the variant the tensor-completion paper is purpose-built for.

tensor-contraction.summary: General tensor-contraction / einsum evaluation, covering four structurally distinct contraction-shape families found in this track's literature: dense multi-operand contraction trees (TCCG + tensor-network applications), small batched irregular fused contractions (knowledge- graph embedding score functions), Kronecker-structured contraction chains, and extreme-scale imbalanced tensor-network contraction (quantum-circuit simulation). No single suite spans all four shape families, so this spec defines one variant per family rather than forcing an artificial common denominator.
tensor-contraction.operation: General form: given tensors {T_1, ..., T_k} and an einsum expression string over multi-indices, compute the output tensor via a sequence of binary contractions (a contraction tree/path), each binary step being C[free_C] = sum_{contracted} A[idx_A] * B[idx_B], with any necessary index permutation performed as part of the same timed step (never amortized out -- see notes_on_fairness).

variants.claim: steady-state kernel throughput on dense multi-operand tensor- contraction trees drawn from the TCCG benchmark and named tensor- network/tensorized-ML applications, index permutation included, fp32
steady-state throughput of small, batched, irregular fused tensor contractions (knowledge-graph-embedding score functions) on real graphs, including the in-kernel runtime index-deduplication cost

steady-state throughput of Kronecker-structured contraction chains (X times the Kronecker product of N factor matrices), a shape distinct enough from general einsum contraction (fixed chain topology, identical small factors) to warrant its own variant, permutation-free by algorithmic design and reported at both precisions

sustained throughput and time-to-solution for extreme-scale, structurally imbalanced tensor-network contraction (random-quantum- circuit simulation), single- and mixed-precision, permutation fully fused into the timed kernel by design

tensor-network.summary: Classical-HPC simulation of quantum circuits, covering two structurally distinct simulation paradigms found in this track's literature: gate-by-gate state-vector/density-matrix propagation (SliQSim, HyQuas, SV-Sim, DM-Sim), where there is no contraction path to search, and genuine tensor-network contraction of a random-quantum-circuit (RQC) tensor network via slicing + contraction-path search (SWQsim). A third variant isolates SliQSim's fundamentally different claim -- exact-arithmetic scalability frontier under a fixed time/memory budget, not steady-state throughput. This track's rqc-tensor-network-contraction variant is deliberately kept consistent (same protocol, same flop-counting convention, same permutation-always-included rule) with the sibling tensor-contraction track's quantum-circuit-contraction-kernel-fp32-mixed variant, which uses the same source paper (SWQsim) as evidence.
tensor-network.operation: General form: given an n-qubit quantum circuit (a sequence of 1- and 2-qubit unitary gates, or, for the density-matrix case, a corresponding sequence of gate-conjugation superoperators), compute either (a) the full final state -- a 2^n-entry state vector or a 2^n x 2^n density matrix -- by applying each gate/superoperator to the current state in circuit order (state-vector/density-matrix paradigm), or (b) a specific amplitude or batch of amplitudes by contracting the tensor network obtained from the circuit's gate graph along a chosen contraction order, optionally with memory-reducing slicing of a subset of the network's edges (tensor-network paradigm). Index permutation required to align tensor operands for a contraction step is always included in the timed step for the tensor-network paradigm (never amortized out), per this track's one point of agreement with the sibling tensor-contraction track.

variants.claim: steady-state per-gate/per-circuit latency and throughput of gate-by-gate state-vector or density-matrix propagation on a standard NISQ-era circuit benchmark suite, single-node and distributed, fp64 by default

sustained throughput and time-to-solution for extreme-scale, structurally imbalanced tensor-network contraction of a random-quantum- circuit (RQC), single- and mixed-precision, contraction-order/slicing search reported separately from execution -- this spec's variant is kept consistent with the sibling tensor-contraction track's quantum-circuit-contraction-kernel-fp32-mixed variant (same source paper, same protocol) since both tracks' literature converges on the identical evidence (SWQsim)

maximum qubit count reachable under EXACT (zero-precision-loss) arithmetic within a fixed wall-clock and memory budget, across structurally distinct circuit families -- a fundamentally different claim from steady-state throughput (variant 1) or sustained FLOP/s (variant 2): this variant measures HOW FAR a method scales before failing, not how fast it runs per gate

tensor-train-decomposition.summary: Tensor-Train (TT) decomposition of an N-mode tensor into a chain of small 3D TT-cores G^(1)..G^(N) such that X[i1..iN] ~= G^(1)[:,i1,:] G^(2)[:,i2,:] ... G^(N)[:,iN,:] (matrix-chain product of the cores' slices). This track's two papers exercise opposite halves of a TT system's lifecycle: STTID DECOMPOSES a given sparse tensor into TT-cores under an accuracy target; EL-Rec never decomposes anything but instead RECONSTRUCTS (TT-core-products) a learned, fixed-TT-rank embedding table on every training step. The spec keeps these as separate variants (see survey.md's Divergences on "decomposition vs. reconstruction timing").
tensor-train-decomposition.operation: Decomposition (STTID): given sparse X[I1..IN] and accuracy target epsilon, compute TT-cores G^(i)[R_{i-1}, I_i, R_i] (R_0=R_N=1) via interpolative/skeleton decomposition such that the relative reconstruction error < epsilon, subject to a rank ceiling R_i <= rmax. Reconstruction (EL-Rec): given trained TT-cores G^(i)[R_{i-1}, q_i, R_i] of fixed rank R_i (a training hyperparameter, not accuracy-derived) and a TT-SHAPE factorization of an embedding index, compute the matrix-chain product on-the-fly for each of many (batch-size) lookups per training step.

variants.claim: steady-state, one-shot sparse-tensor-to-TT-cores decomposition time for a GIVEN accuracy target epsilon, with epsilon and the rank ceiling rmax as required, disclosed parameters (the actual compression-vs-error tradeoff axis this track's papers expose) -- the variant STTID is purpose-built for. TT-rank is reported as an OUTPUT of the run (the per-mode ranks the rank-revealing decomposition actually realized under epsilon), never as a pre-fixed input, matching STTID's own artifact practice.

end-to-end DLRM training throughput using a TT-compressed embedding table of a FIXED, pre-chosen TT-rank (a training hyperparameter, not an accuracy-target output), amortizing the per-lookup TT-core-product "reconstruction" cost over k=1000 training iterations -- the variant EL-Rec is purpose-built for. TT-rank and TT-shape (the factorization of the embedding index/dimension into per-core sizes) are both required, disclosed input parameters here, the reverse of the decomposition variant's rank-as-output convention.

topk-selection.summary: Selecting the k largest elements from a set of n candidates, returned as (value, index) pairs; measured as steady-state exact-selection kernel throughput on a GPU-resident array (the shape this track's most systematically-benchmarked paper actually tests), plus two approximate-search variants — recall-gated ANN top-k over a billion-scale index, and ranking-quality-gated top-k under reduced-precision score computation — that this track's literature treats as genuinely different claims with different correctness models, not size variants of the same benchmark.
topk-selection.operation: topk(scores[n], k) -> (values[k], indices[k]), values sorted descending

variants.claim: exact top-k of a single GPU-resident array, steady-state kernel throughput, single isolated call. The only variant in this track with a mathematically well-defined single "correct" answer (up to tie ordering) — matches AIR Top-K/GridSelect's own benchmark shape, the most systematically-swept paper in this track.

end-to-end approximate-nearest-neighbor top-k query: coarse-quantizer (IVF) search + per-partition candidate scoring + top-k merge across partitions, over a billion-scale real embedding index — UpANNS's own benchmark shape, and the only variant where "n" means total DATASET size rather than a single call's candidate-set size.

approximate top-k over per-query similarity scores computed under REDUCED-PRECISION fixed-point arithmetic (the scores themselves are approximate, not just the search coverage) — Top-K SpMV's own benchmark shape, distinct from topk-e2e-ann-approx because the approximation source is numerical precision of the score computation, not index/search-space coverage, and distinct from topk-array-kernel-exact because correctness is a ranking-quality metric, not exact value-set equality.

transformer-inference-fused.summary: Fully fused transformer encoder layer (QKV projection, multi-head attention, feed-forward network, layer-norm, activation, all in one measured region) for variable-length inputs, executed padding-free so no compute is wasted on pad tokens -- distinct from benchspecs/attention-kernel, which isolates the MHA core alone; this track measures the WHOLE fused layer and requires explicit disclosure of which sub-ops are inside vs. outside the fusion boundary.
transformer-inference-fused.operation: For a variable-length batch of B sequences with per-sequence lengths L_i <= S_max: Encoder(X)[B,S,H] = LayerNorm(X + FFN(LayerNorm(X + MHA(QKV_proj(X))))), where MHA is computed padding-free (each sequence's real L_i tokens only, no wasted work on padding up to S_max), QKV_proj and FFN are dense GEMMs + bias, and the whole N-layer stack (default N=12, BERT-base) is the timed unit unless a single-layer sub-variant is requested.

variants.claim: steady-state latency of the padding-free fused BERT-base encoder (12 layers, all sub-ops -- QKV, MHA, FFN, LN -- inside one measured forward pass), fp16, swept across the batch x sequence-length grid that separates memory-bound small-batch decode-adjacent regimes from compute-bound large-batch/long-sequence regimes. Matches ByteTransformer's own bert_bench.sh sweep.

isolates ONE encoder layer (n_layers=1) rather than the stacked 12-layer forward pass -- lets the per-layer fusion overhead/benefit be measured independent of model depth, and is directly comparable across BERT-base/ALBERT/DistilBERT/DeBERTa-class models of different depths using the same per-layer number.

triangle-counting.summary: Exact global triangle count of a static, undirected, simple graph via edge-orientation + neighbor-intersection; measured as steady-state counting throughput with orientation/format-conversion preprocessing reported separately, across single-GPU and MPI-distributed-CPU variants that the surveyed literature treats as genuinely different regimes (no paper in this track straddles both platforms).
triangle-counting.operation: T = |{(u,v,w) : uv,vw,wu in E}| for undirected simple graph G=(V,E); computed via a directed orientation of each edge (typically low-degree -> high-degree, i.e. degree ordering / DODGR construction) followed by local set-intersection of directed out-neighborhoods, summed and, depending on the orientation convention, divided by a small constant (1, 3, or 6) to yield the unique undirected triangle count.

variants.claim: steady-state single-GPU counting-kernel throughput, graph already resident in device memory in the algorithm's native format (CSR / DCSR / bitmap / tensor-core layout); orientation and any format-specific reordering conversion EXCLUDED from the timed region but reported separately. The common denominator TC-Compare/GroupTC's own 9-algorithm harness and ToT's per-phase CUDATimer split both actually measure.

end-to-end single-GPU throughput including one-shot CSR build + orientation + algorithm-native format conversion, amortized over k=100 repeated counts on the same resident graph — TC-Compare's own 100-iteration convention read as an amortization count rather than a pure-kernel repetition count, and the realistic "load graph once, count many times" usage pattern implied by streaming/dynamic-graph follow-on work in this space.

distributed-memory strong-scaling wall-clock time on a fixed real-world graph across a core-count ladder; I/O + graph distribution EXCLUDED and reported separately (matching all 3 distributed papers), edge orientation / degree-ordering REPORTED AS ITS OWN SEPARATE NUMBER even though 2 of 3 surveyed distributed papers (katric, likely lcc) bundle it into the counted time — following TriPoll's cleaner preprocess_timer/step_timer split as the fairness fix.

distributed-memory weak-scaling wall-clock time on Graph500-style R-MAT synthetic graphs with fixed edges-per-core, across a core-count ladder — covers the RMAT/KaGen-generated instances all 3 distributed papers (and TC-Compare, single-GPU) use for scale sweeps, using the OFFICIAL Graph500 R-MAT parameters as the single shared generator definition since the 3 papers' own scale ladders (katric n=16-18, lcc S21/S23/S30, TriPoll up to scale 32) don't otherwise overlap.

trsm.summary: Triangular solve with multiple right-hand sides (TRSM), covering both a standalone single-call kernel across the full side/uplo/trans/diag layout matrix and a uniform-shape batched-CPU variant — the two claims this track's only TRSM microbenchmark (fBLAS) actually exercises. Distributed mixed-precision TRSM fused inside a Cholesky-based solver (this track's other paper, AbdulahCPBDGKLS22) is out of scope for a single-kernel benchmark spec; see notes_on_fairness and open_questions.
trsm.operation: solve op(A)[N,N] * X = alpha*B[N,M]  (side=Left)  or  X * op(A)[N,N] = alpha*B[N,M]  (side=Right), A triangular (uplo in {Lower, Upper}), op(A) in {A, A^T} (trans in {NoTrans, Trans}), diag in {NonUnit, Unit}; result X overwrites B in place.

variants.claim: steady-state throughput of a single (non-batched) TRSM call, reported across the FULL side x uplo x trans layout matrix (diag=NonUnit) — not just the one Left/Lower/NoTrans configuration fBLAS's own paper publishes performance numbers for, even though fBLAS's own artifact already builds and functionally tests all 8 layout combinations per precision (`tests/host_api/trsm.json`). This closes the gap between fBLAS's functional test coverage (8 layouts x 2 precisions = 16 configs) and its performance-reporting coverage (1 config).

steady-state throughput of uniform-shape batched TRSM (same N, M across the batch, side=Left/uplo=Lower/trans=NoTrans/diag=NonUnit, independent problems), reproducing fBLAS's own CPU/MKL batched benchmark harness (`evaluation/cpu_programs/batched_trsm.cpp`) verbatim in problem shape but replacing its 1-run-discarded / best-of- thread-sweep statistic with a proper warmup+repetition protocol.

tucker.summary: Tucker decomposition of an N-mode sparse tensor: X ~= G x1 A^(1) x2 A^(2) ... xN A^(N), where G is a small dense core tensor and A^(i) are dense factor matrices, computed iteratively (HOSVD/HOOI/HOQRI). This track's two papers exercise opposite ends of that iteration: SymProp optimizes the per-iteration TTMc/TTMc-chain KERNEL for symmetric sparse tensors, while SGD_Tucker optimizes the whole SGD-driven DECOMPOSITION LOOP (mini-batch ALS-style updates) for general sparse tensors. The spec keeps these as separate variants rather than forcing one iteration semantics across both (see survey.md Divergences).
tucker.operation: G[R1..RN], A^(i)[I_i,R_i] (i=1..N) such that X[I1..IN] ~= sum_{r1..rN} G[r1..rN] * A^(1)[:,r1] o A^(2)[:,r2] o ... o A^(N)[:,rN] (outer product), computed via alternating per-mode TTMc contractions (S3TTMc / S3TTMcTC when the input is symmetric, so only one canonical mode's contraction needs computing per sweep) followed by a small core/factor update (HOOI power-iteration or HOQRI QR-based step, or a stochastic-gradient mini-batch update as in SGD_Tucker).

variants.claim: steady-state per-sweep S3TTMc/S3TTMcTC kernel throughput exploiting full input symmetry (single canonical-mode contraction suffices per HOOI/HOQRI sweep, not N), preprocessing (CSS format construction) excluded and reported separately once. This is the variant SymProp is purpose-built for; it directly reuses this project's mttkrp track's mttkrp-symmetric-kernel-fp64 input suite and rank sweep, since S3TTMc/S3TTMcTC are the same symmetric-contraction kernel family surveyed there for the Tucker/HOOI/HOQRI use case specifically (as opposed to that track's CP-ALS use case).

end-to-end sparse Tucker decomposition wall-clock time to reach a target relative reconstruction error (or, if the reconstruction-error target is not reached, wall-clock time for a fixed, disclosed iteration budget k), on general (asymmetric) real sparse tensors -- the variant SGD_Tucker's own evaluation style maps onto. Unlike the kernel variant above, "iteration" here means one full decomposition sweep (one HOOI power-iteration OR one SGD mini-batch update, whichever the system under test implements), NOT a single TTMc kernel call -- the two are not interchangeable (see survey.md Divergences).

vertex-cover.summary: Exact GPU-parallel branch-and-bound search for Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC) and Parameterized Vertex Cover (PVC, cover size <= k) on small-to-medium undirected graphs, measured as search-tree wall time on a fixed mixed suite of adversarial and real-world instances, with exact-optimum correctness (this is an EXACT combinatorial problem, not an approximation) as the hard gate before any timing counts.
vertex-cover.operation: cover[V] subset of V = VertexCover(A[V,V] adjacency (sparse, undirected), mode in {MVC, k}); output is a vertex subset S such that every edge has at least one endpoint in S; MVC minimizes |S|, PVC decides/returns S with |S| <= k for a given k. A is unweighted, undirected, simple (no self-loops/multi-edges after preprocessing).

variants.claim: steady-state GPU search-tree wall time to find the EXACT minimum vertex cover on a fixed mixed suite of adversarial and real-world graphs; the search-tree exploration itself is the entire timed region (there is no separable "preprocessing" phase for this problem beyond CSR/adjacency-list construction, which is one-shot and reported separately)

steady-state GPU search-tree wall time to DECIDE, for a given parameter k, whether a vertex cover of size <= k exists (and return one if so) — the parameterized decision variant, timed separately from MVC-search because PVC's early-termination behavior (it can stop as soon as ANY size-k cover is found, or prove none exists) gives it a qualitatively different time profile than exhaustive minimization

winograd.summary: Latency and throughput of Winograd/Cook-Toom fast convolution for 3x3 stride-1 layers, measured with an algorithm-invariant flop convention and with the numerical error the transform introduces reported as a first-class result rather than left unstated.
winograd.operation: Y = A^T [ (G g G^T) (*) (B^T d B) ] A  for output tile F(m,r): filter g is r x r (r = 3), input tile d is (m+r-1) x (m+r-1), (*) is element-wise multiply. Direct-equivalent output: standard 3x3 stride-1 convolution over NCHW input.

variants.claim: steady-state convolution-layer throughput of a Winograd implementation at a disclosed tile size, comparable against direct/im2col/FFT convolution because the flop convention is algorithm-invariant
the speed/accuracy frontier across tile sizes, which is the actual decision a deployer makes and which a single latency number hides
whole-network inference latency, the number a mobile deployer experiences, including the layers Winograd does not apply to
